item.title: Mean-Tilted Intervals: Regression and Dynamic Models
item.description: arXiv:2610.13960v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Mean-tilted intervals (MTIs) provide a fixed-content family of interval targets indexed by retained-mean balance. This paper develops generalized-Bayes computation for using those targets in regression and time-varying endpoint models after content and tilt have been specified. The update combines a prior with an exponentiated residual-product check loss, yielding uncertainty summaries for endpoint functions rather than a response-distribution model. A pseudo-asymmetric-Laplace normal-exponential representation gives generalized-inverse-Gaussian latent-scale updates and Gaussian conditional updates for one root when the other is fixed. The same representation gives deterministic ECM equations for generalized-posterior modes. We present ridge endpoint regression, a conditionally Gaussian shrinkage construction for the zero-tilt case, deterministic fixed-feature readouts, and dynamic linear endpoint states updated by alternating forward-filtering backward-sampling steps. These methods extend the MTI target from iid intervals to regression and dynamic settings; tolerance certification and response prediction require separate calibration or response models.
item.dc:creator: Antonio De Leon, Raquel Prado, Bruno Sans\'o

item.title: Reference-State Bootstrap Correction and Kernel Characterization of Residual-Based Fit Indices in Structural Equation Models
item.description: arXiv:2610.13968v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Sampling error affects the finite-sample values of residual-based fit indices. We show that the unweighted comparative fit index ($CFI_u$) rests on a quadratic-kernel maximum mean discrepancy and that a Gaussian-kernel comparative fit index (KCFI) converges to $CFI_u$ as bandwidth increases. Because kernel discrepancies lack an analytic sampling correction, we extend expected-discrepancy bootstrap methods to a fitted-correlation reference state: the sample is transformed to reproduce the fitted correlation matrix, then resampled and refitted to estimate the exact-fit sampling component. Across 18 confirmatory factor analysis conditions, this correction reduced the root mean square error (RMSE) of both indices by 62%-87%. Under normality it matched an analytic residual-covariance estimator of $CFI_u$ within .0001, and in small samples it outperformed ordinary bootstrap correction in accuracy and availability. Corrected KCFI had lower RMSE than identically corrected $CFI_u$ in all 29 nonnormal conditions, even against a common target, but in six heavy-tailed small-sample conditions the analytic estimator was more accurate than both. The results validate the reference-state correction where it is needed and delimit where the analytic estimator is preferable.
item.dc:creator: Eunjeong Song, Sehee Hong

item.title: Dynamic Extended Generalized Many-Facet Rasch Model: A Unified Approach to Rater-Mediated Assessment
item.description: arXiv:2610.14199v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Rating procedures are crucial in psychological and medical diagnosis, educational assessment, peer review, and grant evaluation. A major methodological challenge is disentangling multiple sources of variability in ratings, such as subject ability, rater behavior, and item characteristics. Item Response Theory-based models, most notably many-facet Rasch models and hierarchical rater models, have been widely adopted for jointly estimating subject, rater, and item effects, while retaining high interpretability. We introduce the Dynamic Extended Generalized Many-Facet Rasch model, a general class of Bayesian semiparametric models that integrate and extend existing approaches. Its measurement model allows location and discrimination parameters to depend jointly on item and rater characteristics and incorporates subject-item and rater-subject variation. The dynamic extension introduces a rater-specific cross-lagged effect capturing dependence on the previously rated subject, and a Bayesian P-spline capturing systematic changes in discrimination over the rating sequence, accounting for learning, fatigue, or adaptation effects. Subject heterogeneity is addressed through Bayesian nonparametric mixtures, flexibly learning the latent ability distribution without strict parametric assumptions and enabling model-based subject clustering. We also derive a closed-form, model-based inter-rater consensus coefficient and study its characteristics. We discuss theoretical properties, develop posterior computation strategies, and evaluate the model in simulation studies and two real-data applications.
item.dc:creator: Giuseppe Mignemi, Patr\'icia Martinkov\'a, Sally Paganin

item.title: cvxoptdes: convex optimal experiment design in R
item.description: arXiv:2610.14288v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The cvxoptdes R-package provides a unified framework to perform convex optimal experiment design and online response optimization for linear, generalized linear and additive, nonlinear, and random intercept mixed models, using exclusively open-source solvers. It supports optimization and augmentation of weighted, penalized and convex constrained continuous designs across a discrete grid of candidate points and rounding to integer-valued designs using point-exchange algorithms or mixed-integer programming for orthogonally constrained designs, including the class of orthogonal minimally aliased response surface (OMARS) designs. Models and design constraints are defined and updated in an object-oriented context with the aim to facilitate the process of sequential (penalized) design augmentation analogous to online design procedures known from active learning and Bayesian optimization.
item.dc:creator: Joris Chau, Alexandre Segers, Martin Otava, Stephen Karanja

item.title: De-biased Distribution Estimation for Locally Differential Private Survival Data
item.description: arXiv:2610.14320v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Sharing time-to-event data can leak sensitive information about individual participants in clinical studies. To protect the privacy of data, differential privacy (DP) framework offers rigorous protection for data sharing. The local variant of differential privacy is particularly appealing because each record is perturbed before it leaves the data owner or contributor. However, the injected perturbation distorts the true distribution of the source data, yielding low utility and invalid statistical inference with the released data. In this work, we propose a nonparametric estimator for the true survivor function via the deconvolution kernel function with locally differential private (LDP) right-censored survival data in which both the event times and the event indicators are privatized. Our estimator simultaneously de-biases the perturbation applied to the times and the errors induced by flipping the event indicators due to LDP. Theoretically, we establish the uniform consistency and point-wise asymptotic normality of the de-biased distribution estimator, and derive its uniform convergence rate together with the optimal bandwidth attaining that rate. Simulation studies and the analysis of a semi-synthetic dataset generated from the METABRIC breast cancer cohort demonstrate the performance of the proposed estimator across privacy budgets, censoring levels, and sample sizes. By the post-processing property of DP, the proposed de-biased estimator inherits the privacy guarantee while restoring valid inference on the survivor function.
item.dc:creator: Yi Xiong, Li-Pang Chen, Liyue Fan

item.title: Sharp bounds for population and principal effects under latent sequential ignorability
item.description: arXiv:2610.14330v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Treatment decisions are often sequential and depend on information absent from the recorded history. Latent sequential ignorability models such assignment by assuming that baseline covariates and principal strata, defined by joint potential intermediate responses, account for confounding of later treatment. For two treatment periods with a binary intermediate response, we derive sharp population and principal effect bounds under a specified association between the potential responses and show that the two targets can require different optimizations to obtain sharp bounds. For population effects, optimization over latent treatment probabilities reduces to their feasible endpoints. Stronger selection between response types can be offset by making their outcome distributions more similar, preserving both the observed distribution and population marginal outcome distributions. This replacement can change effects within principal strata, whose sharp bounds may instead require interior treatment probabilities. Restrictions on differences in conditional effects can tighten the bounds without equating outcome levels. For binary outcomes, we give an exact finite algorithm that includes these interior assignments. We also develop inference under smoothness and estimation conditions. We illustrate the bounds in a study of gym attendance after an incentive program.
item.dc:creator: Yuki Ohnishi

item.title: Global Inference for High Dimensional Quantile Regression with Heterogeneity
item.description: arXiv:2610.14347v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Quantile regression has received considerable attention in high dimensional methodology due to its robustness and ability to accommodate heteroskedasticity. Despite this attention, current inferential methods for high dimensional quantile regression have significant limitations---only testing significance, testing at a single quantile at a time, or assuming homoskedasticity. To generalize the inferences that can be drawn in high dimensional quantile regression, we introduce partial penalized Wald and rank score tests for testing linear hypotheses uniformly over a set of quantiles $\mathcal T$ under a heteroskedastic model. We propose globally adaptive local linear approximation (LLA) algorithms for folded concave penalized estimation and show that our global LLA algorithms recover ``testing oracles'' for the full and reduced models with high probability. We then show that our global LLA estimators achieve the $\sqrt{s/n}$ oracle estimation rate uniformly over $\mathcal T$, establish Bahadur representations, and derive asymptotic distributions for the test statistics under the null and local alternatives. We develop a dual formulation incorporating adaptive penalty weights for the rank scores and use the strong oracle property to establish their oracle equivalence. Using empirical process techniques, we derive reference distributions based on suprema of squared Bessel processes, extending partial penalized inference beyond pointwise chi-square calibration.
item.dc:creator: Tate Jacobson, Daeyoung Ham, Ben Sherwood

item.title: Decomposing the spectral density function of an ARMA process
item.description: arXiv:2610.14384v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Quasi-periodic oscillations are characterized by fitting Lorentzian functions to a nonparametric estimate of the power spectral density, a two-step procedure that separates estimation from modeling and does not accommodate measurement error. We develop a parametric alternative based on autoregressive moving-average (ARMA) processes observed with measurement error. We derive an exact decomposition of the ARMA spectral density into real-valued components, one for each class of autoregressive roots under complex conjugation, plus a polynomial term when the moving-average order is at least the autoregressive order. Each component is a Wrapped Cauchy kernel, and for complex roots it is accompanied by a conjugate-Poisson term that makes the peak asymmetric and displaces its maximum from the frequency given by the argument of the root. We obtain closed-form expressions for the location, height, width, and asymmetry of each peak, and a matching variance decomposition. Parameters are estimated by maximum likelihood through the Kalman filter, and all descriptors follow by plug-in. Simulations show that the closed-form peak location is recovered without appreciable bias. An X-ray binary light curve illustrates the methodology.
item.dc:creator: Darlin Soto-V\'asquez, Francisco Cuevas-Pacheco, Giovanni Motta, Malgorzata Sobolewska

item.title: The Quantification of Replicability
item.description: arXiv:2610.14407v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: What does it mean to measure the replicability of scientific results? Is it merely determining whether results are consistent across studies? Much of the existing literature on replicability draws conclusions exclusively from the comparison of study results, in terms of observed estimates, uses a variety of different metrics, and ultimately collapses the comparison into a binary verdict of success or failure. This fails to differentiate between repeated errors and corroboration of the shared generative effect. We develop a unified Bayesian framework in which distinct but related notions of replicability are formally defined and jointly embedded within a single inferential structure. A single model answers four complementary questions: agreement among independent studies; consistency between the individual studies and the shared generative effect; agreement between an existing body of evidence and a new study from the same super-population; inference on the shared generative effect. In practice, we suggest quantifying replicability through posterior probabilities relative to regions of practical relevance. We illustrate these ideas in an eQTL (expression quantitative trait locus) analysis assessing the replicability of a regulatory effect across human ancestral groups.
item.dc:creator: Ester Alongi, Gianmarco Alto\`e, Giovanni Parmigiani

item.title: Prior-Informed Generalizable Low-Rank Representation Learning via Regularized Adversarial Reweighting
item.description: arXiv:2610.14414v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Modern learning problems increasingly leverage data from heterogeneous sources to improve robustness and generalizability under distribution shift, often with high-dimensional parameters admitting low-rank structure. Existing group distributionally robust optimization (group-DRO) approaches optimize against adverse source mixtures, but extending this principle to low-rank matrix estimation with a broad class of losses leads to a challenging nonconvex-concave problem for which methods and theory remain limited. We propose Prior-Informed generalizable Low-rank representation Learning via Adversarial Reweighting (PILLAR), which smooths the group-DRO objective by regularizing adversarial source weights toward a user-specified reference distribution while learning a shared low-rank representation. By tempering extreme adversarial reweighting, PILLAR improves estimation stability and reduces the potential conservativeness of group-DRO. Using Burer-Monteiro factorization, we optimize the nonconvex-concave objective by bifactored gradient descent with mirror ascent. We establish linear convergence to a statistical neighborhood of the population saddle point and derive an error bound that separates low-rank estimation from adversarial reweighting. We further show that PILLAR improves on vanilla group DRO when the latter's excess conservativeness dominates source heterogeneity and prior misspecification. Simulations and an electronic health record study of suicide-attempt risk demonstrate improved worst-source and transported predictive accuracy.
item.dc:creator: Keyao Zhan, Junwei Lu, Tianxi Cai

item.title: Copula Active Subspaces II: Error Decomposition, A Posteriori Estimation, and Sharpness of the Bounds
item.description: arXiv:2610.14498v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The Copula Active Subspaces (CAS) method of Part I estimates a non-Gaussian observation-noise density $\pi_{\boldsymbol{n}}$ from residual samples. Its KL divergence $\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{KL}}(\pi_{\boldsymbol{n}}\,\|\,\widehat\pi_{\boldsymbol{n}})$ admits an exact decomposition into marginal, projection and reduced-density terms and bounds the posterior KL divergence averaged over the true predictive distribution. We derive a priori bounds for these terms, together with estimates or bounds from residual samples. Weighted nearest-neighbour entropy estimates are used for the marginal and reduced-density terms, with asymptotic standard errors in exact rank coordinates. For the projection error, the score is fitted on one subsample, and its mean squared magnitude outside the retained subspace is estimated on the other. Corrections for score and rank-transform errors then give a theoretical upper bound with probability at least $1-\delta$. Tests on three known noise laws in dimension $d=20$ use the estimated rank transform. In $11$ of $12$ combinations of example and sample size, the sum of the two estimated terms and the trace bound exceeds the reference divergence after averaging over the estimated models. In these tests, score-estimation error is the largest contribution to looseness. The overestimate from the Gaussian log-Sobolev inequality alone is at most a factor of $1.98$.
item.dc:creator: Joshua Chen, Peter Jan van Leeuwen

item.title: Identification and Estimation of Treatment Effects from Network Data with Confounded Social Links
item.description: arXiv:2610.14527v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In observational network data, the adoption of a treatment and the formation of social ties often depend on the same characteristics that affect outcomes. We propose a generalized propensity score for each unit's effective treatment, built from a model for treatment assignment and a dyadic model for network formation, which may include latent node heterogeneity. The score is marginalized over the network given covariates rather than conditioned on the realized network, and the estimand is a population effect: the average effect of an exposure level for a unit drawn from the population of units and networks. We relate this estimand to those of methods that condition on the realized network and show what marginalizing costs and buys. It requires network formation to be unconfounded given observed covariates, a stronger assumption than unconfoundedness of treatment given the network. In exchange, it defines effects at exposure levels that poorly connected units cannot reach, and at levels every unit can reach it gives an estimator whose asymptotic variance is no larger than the network-conditional one. We combine the score with an augmented inverse probability weighting estimator, prove asymptotic normality as the number of networks grows with bounded network size, discuss what carries over to a single large sparse network, and apply the method to the effect of a political communication technology on political participation in Uganda.
item.dc:creator: Licheng Liu

item.title: Cointegrated Regressors: Where Folded Concave Penalties Go Beyond LASSO
item.description: arXiv:2610.14617v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: LASSO is one of the most popular regularization methods for high-dimensional regression models. While cointegration is common in practical applications of predictive regressions with many regressors, the convex penalty of LASSO overly suppresses the coefficients of cointegrated regressors and therefore fails to deliver consistent parameter estimation. We employ folded concave penalties (FCP), including the well-known SCAD and MCP, to address this issue. Using FCP, we establish two asymptotic results: (i) a local oracle property for the penalized regression, and (ii) a global oracle property for regressions with a penalty-level constraint. In particular, the latter guarantees a global solution that consistently estimates the true coefficients and enjoys oracle prediction performance. Simulation studies and an application to predicting the euro area unemployment rate show that FCP improves variable selection and out-of-sample prediction relative to LASSO.
item.dc:creator: Hongqi Chen, Chengwang Liao, Ziwei Mei, Zhentao Shi

item.title: The price of a weak shadow variable: inference under nonignorable missingness as relevance vanishes
item.description: arXiv:2610.14695v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: When an outcome is missing not at random, identification is commonly restored by a shadow variable: a covariate that predicts the outcome but is excluded from the response mechanism. The literature treats the first requirement, relevance, as a yes-or-no condition. We make it continuous, parametrizing it by a scalar that scales the shadow variable's entire contribution to the moment conditions, and ask what inference costs as that scalar vanishes. One functional of the inverse weight governs the answer. We characterize it exactly, show that it fixes the effective sample size, and use it to sharpen the rates of the estimator that avoids the weight. The characterization is concrete. Whether the functional saturates or diverges turns not on boundedness of the outcome but on whether the tilting variable has an atom at its essential supremum: a binary outcome saturates, a uniform one does not. It also bounds how far a scanned set reaches, and that reach grows only as the square root of the logarithm of the sample size, so a thousandfold increase buys one unit of tilt while the set to be scanned widens without limit.
item.dc:creator: Michael B\"ucker

item.title: An Unscented PrO Kalman Filter
item.description: arXiv:2610.14773v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Predictively-oriented (PrO) filtering for state-space models was proposed in Shen et al. [2026] as a promising route to avoiding over-confident inferences in settings where either the dynamical model, the measurement model, or both, could be misspecified. Our focus is on nonlinear state-space models, where the local linearisation used to construct the PrO filter in Shen et al. [2026] deteriorates as nonlinearities enter either the dynamical model or the measurement model. Our proposed solution is based on unscented transforms, an established tool from classical filtering which provides a more accurate mechanism to propagate Gaussian uncertainty through a nonlinear functional, and which includes the cubature rule as a special case. We introduce two variants: replacing the linearisation in the predict step alone, which we call UKF-PrO, has a computational cost comparable to the existing PrO filter; replacing it in the update step as well, UKF-PrO+, requires a substantially more expensive joint optimisation. Performance is empirically assessed on the Lorenz96 model under conditions of increasing difficulty, in which the state-space model is systematically misspecified; we find that UKF-PrO with the parameters of the cubature Kalman filter offers consistent improvements, which become substantial under strong nonlinearity, whereas the default unscented parameters are unreliable, and that the full update-step extension with the same parameters does not justify its additional cost.
item.dc:creator: Dan Kean, Zheyang Shen, Chris. J. Oates

item.title: Comparing randomized trials
item.description: arXiv:2610.14895v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Disagreements between randomized trials that address the same causal question pose challenges for the interpretation and synthesis of evidence. We sketch a causal framework for comparing the results of randomized trials that explicitly accommodates the possibility of trial engagement effects. Using counterfactual outcomes defined under joint interventions on treatment assignment and trial-related actions, we compare trial-native treatment effects with the effects transported from one trial to the population of another in a common target population. We show that standard conditions for transporting treatment effects across trial populations are not sufficient to guarantee agreement between transported and trial-native effects. Agreement additionally requires conditions governing how trial-related actions affect outcome across studies - for example, absence of trial engagement effects, equivalence of such effects across trials, or lack of interaction between trial engagement and treatment assignment. Our framework clarifies potential sources of disagreement across trials and extends existing approaches to study comparison to settings in which trial engagement effects may be present.
item.dc:creator: Yu-Han Chiu, Issa J. Dahabreh

item.title: An Algebraic Approach to Constrained K-means Clustering
item.description: arXiv:2610.14932v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Clustering is typically performed using only object features, although additional information about relationships between objects may be available and can be incorporated through constraints. Among these, pairwise constraints require two objects to belong to the same cluster or to different clusters. Several extensions of the k-means algorithm accommodate such constraints, but they sometimes fail to find a feasible assignment or incur high computational cost. Motivated by these limitations, we propose an algebraic approach to k-means clustering with pairwise constraints. The algorithm simplifies the constraints using Gr\"{o}bner bases before optimization, improving the efficiency of cluster assignment. It can also detect whether the constraint set has a feasible assignment before optimization. Comparative experiments with existing algorithms showed that the proposed algorithm achieved comparable or better clustering quality at a lower computational cost, particularly when the numbers of constraints and clusters were small.
item.dc:creator: Hiroki Oohori, Kentaro Fukushima, Michio Yamamoto

item.title: Bayesian adaptive design for neural recruitment curves
item.description: arXiv:2610.15000v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Nonlinear response models remain ubiquitous across disciplines with recruitment curves describing muscle response to neural stimulation. Conventional acquisition methods typically rely on static uniform sampling, requiring many stimuli, while adaptive threshold-hunting designs such as ML-PEST forfeit accurate characterization of the overall curve. We present a Bayesian adaptive design that uses posterior uncertainty over curve parameters to propose stimuli that maximize information gain across the full recruitment curve. We additionally implement a focused acquisition method that can target arbitrary subset of curve parameters, which we use to evaluate and interpret our design. In simulations, our design outperforms uniform sampling in recovering threshold while matching ML-PEST, and outperforms ML-PEST in predictive curve accuracy while matching uniform. It likewise matches our threshold-focused acquisition, suggesting our design doesn't trade off threshold estimation for recovering the curve. We further show data collected using our design yields greater power when detecting a change in threshold in intervention studies. Our design proposes the next stimulus within 5 seconds, making it feasible for transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS) experiments. Finally, we validate our design in TMS experiments and provide a library for Python, called onMEP, for online acquisition of neural recruitment curves.
item.dc:creator: Vishweshwar Tyagi, Saihari S. Dukkipati, Daniel Twili, Jonas M. Mikhaeil, Andrew Gelman, Jason B. Carmel, James R. McIntosh

item.title: Rate-Based Causal Discovery for Heavy-Tailed Models
item.description: arXiv:2610.15051v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In many complex systems, such as river networks and financial markets, extreme events propagate from causes to their effects, and the largest observations carry the most information about the underlying causal structure. Existing methods for causal discovery in extremes, however, are tailored to specific mechanisms, such as linear or max-linear models. This work develops causal discovery for heavy-tailed homogeneous structural causal models, a flexible class that contains linear, max-linear and norm-type mechanisms, which may differ from node to node. In these models, the causal structure is encoded by ancestral impulse responses, which measure how a shock at one node is transmitted to its descendants. We propose the extremal minimum ratio estimator of these responses, which uses only observations in which the potential cause is extreme. The estimator is consistent under regular variation alone, and we derive its exact rates of convergence and limiting distributions, which depend on both the causal relation and the type of mechanism. Building on these rates, we construct consistent estimators of the causal order and of the full set of ancestral relations, using a threshold that adapts to the data and requires no knowledge of the tail index. The method is illustrated on simulated data and on river discharges in the upper Danube basin.
item.dc:creator: Vishal Routh

item.title: A Cosine-Projection Framework for Choosing Among Cox HR, D-RMST, and Average-Hazard Tests in Survival Trials
item.description: arXiv:2610.15149v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The log-rank/Cox hazard-ratio test remains the standard approach for the primary analysis of randomized trials with time-to-event endpoints and is fully efficient under proportional hazards (PH). Two model-free alternatives that have recently gained attention are the difference in restricted mean survival time (D-RMST), a contrast on the time scale, and the more recently proposed ratio of average hazards (RAH), a contrast on the rate scale. Simulation studies suggest that the RAH-based test can outperform both under delayed treatment effects, but its efficiency has not been characterized analytically, and no unified framework explains how censoring and accrual affect the efficiency ordering among these tests. We show that all three statistics share a weighted-log-rank representation and derive their asymptotic relative efficiencies under local alternatives, including the first analytic efficiency results for the RAH-based test. Geometrically, each test defines a direction in a function space and the anticipated treatment effect defines a signal direction. A test's efficiency relative to the oracle test equals the squared cosine of the angle between these directions, so the asymptotic relative efficiency of any two tests is a ratio of squared cosines. Because censoring and accrual enter through an information weight, the framework shows how design choices can alter, and even reverse, the efficiency ordering. We illustrate the framework using the CheckMate 057 immunotherapy trial and corroborate the theoretical results through simulations spanning proportional- and non-proportional-hazards settings.
item.dc:creator: Xiang Meng, Lu Tian, Hajime Uno

item.title: Closed forms all the way up: the sample variance of four observations
item.description: arXiv:2610.15174v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The distribution function $F(y)=\Pr(S^2\le y)$ of the sample variance $S^2$ of four independent observations is elementary on its entire support for every polynomial parent density on $[0,1]$ (without loss of generality), and we give it in finite closed form for the uniform, Beta$(2,1)$ and Beta$(2,2)$ parents. The support splits at $y = 1/6$, $2/9$ and $1/4$, with the ceiling at $1/3$, all fixed by geometry: in coordinates aligned with the cube diagonal the event $S^2\le y$ is a ball of radius $\sqrt{3y}$, the cube projects to a rhombic dodecahedron, and these are the levels at which the ball reaches its faces, edges and two kinds of vertices. The divergence theorem reduces every moment of the clipped ball to integrals along circular arcs, so each regime closes in algebraic functions of $\sqrt{y}$ and inverse trigonometric functions. For the uniform parent the only non-obvious constant is $K_g = 12\sqrt2\arctan\sqrt2$, proportional to the mean width of the cuboctahedron; the Beta constants are rational expressions in $\pi$, $\sqrt2$, $\sqrt3$ and $\arctan\sqrt2$, as in the uniform case. At $n = 4$ the normal-theory $\chi^2$ recipe used in acceptance testing misplaces the $99$th percentile of $S^2$ by $50\%$ for the uniform parent. For three observations, polynomial parents also give elementary closed forms (arXiv:2609.25333), but two elementary cases in a row do not guarantee a third, and we make no claim beyond $n = 4$.
item.dc:creator: Remus Osan

item.title: Precision follows the decision: how well an acceptance probability is known for mean-spread release rules
item.description: arXiv:2610.15194v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Many release rules accept a lot when a statistic built from the sample mean and standard deviation stays within a limit, and the probability that a process passes such a rule can be computed exactly for a broad class of parent distributions. This paper asks how well that probability is itself known once the parent has been estimated. Under a stated reference posterior the answer is an interval, narrow where a lot clearly passes or fails and wide where it is contested. In ninety-eight published content-uniformity lots that position, not the sample size, sets the width: among the forty-eight lots assayed at the same ten units, and so equally informed about the spread, the $95\%$ interval runs from essentially zero width to $0.96$. With the operating point held fixed while test and estimation sample grow together, the interval narrows only slowly, the contraction of the posterior being offset by the steepening of the operating characteristic; a calibrated study at the sample sizes of $1207$ occupational exposure assessments shows the same under a half-plane rule. For a pure-spread rule under a Normal parent the interval has an exact chi-square form in the plug-in value and the two sample sizes, extending to the mean-spread wedge with a measured residual and containing Bergum's lower bound as one endpoint. With the parent's posterior formed from the same published summaries through the evaluator's own likelihood, the qualitative pattern survives but shape moves both endpoints and width: on the same lots a strong right skew lowers the pessimistic endpoint by up to a fifth and widens the interval by up to $0.22$. At the content-uniformity operating point studied, under a Normal parent, the symmetric error bar in standard use puts the lower endpoint $0.21$ too high and returns an upper endpoint above one, even with the full posterior covariance.
item.dc:creator: Remus Osan

item.title: Stable Causal Estimation with Optimal Transport
item.description: arXiv:2610.15212v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In observational studies, the overlap assumption, also called positivity, is frequently strained in practice. Limited overlap destabilizes widely used estimators such as inverse propensity weighting (IPW), whose variance depends on density ratios that explode as propensity scores approach zero or one. To address this challenge, we propose the Stable Transport Estimator (STE), an optimal transport-based approach for estimating average causal effects when overlap holds but strict overlap fails. Unlike IPW, the variance of STE contains no density-ratio factor; it is governed by the transport map itself and stays finite under bounded moments, even when density ratios diverge. By replacing reweighting with a geometry-aware transport map, STE constructs stable counterfactual comparisons without requiring density estimation or propensity score modeling. STE further extends to settings where the overlap condition is violated: when covariate supports overlap only partially, a linear interpolation transport map enables principled extrapolation with explicit bias-variance trade-offs. We establish consistency, asymptotic normality, and a variance characterization that makes explicit the contribution of the estimated transport map to the asymptotic variance. Across synthetic and real datasets, STE demonstrates improved robustness, reduced bias, and markedly more stable variance compared to existing estimators.
item.dc:creator: Yidan Xu, Yixin Wang, XuanLong Nguyen

item.title: Moment-Calibrated Conformal Prediction with Side Information
item.description: arXiv:2610.15268v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: For a fixed conformal score function, standard split conformal prediction calibrates a prediction set using the empirical distribution of the conformal scores, without using available side information about the data. We propose a moment-calibrated approach that uses such information to reduce variability across calibration data sets. Side information involving the covariates, the response, or both is expressed as moment restrictions, which are enforced through empirical likelihood weights on the calibration data points. The resulting weighted empirical distribution of the scores determines the weighted empirical quantile without changing the score function. We establish finite-sample bounds on training-conditional and marginal coverage of the moment-calibrated prediction set. We derive asymptotic distributions for training-conditional coverage and average prediction-set size, show that their asymptotic variances are no larger than the corresponding variances under standard split conformal prediction, and characterize when the reductions are strict. In the semi-supervised setting, we identify an optimal moment function of a given covariate representation, develop implementations using prespecified moment functions or a function learned by cross-fitting, and quantify the effect of the unlabeled sample size. We also extend the method to coverage conditions indexed by a class of functions of the covariates through weighted quantile regression. Numerical studies demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed methods.
item.dc:creator: Guanghui Wang, Liuhua Peng, Liu Liu, Changliang Zou

item.title: Approximation, Consistency, and Prediction in Generalized Neural Network Mixed Models for Longitudinal and Clustered Data
item.description: arXiv:2610.15270v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Generalized neural network mixed models (GNMMs) combine neural networks and mixed-effects models to analyze longitudinal and clustered data. Although GNMMs have shown good predictive performance in practice, their statistical properties are not well understood. Therefore, this paper studies several important properties of GNMM and provides theoretical support for its use. First, we show that the neural-network component can approximate an unknown nonlinear fixed-effect function arbitrarily well and establish consistency of the fitted neural- network function for its population target within a given network class. Next, we establish consistency of random-effect estimation under increasing within-subject information and show that the GNMM predictor converges to the true predictor. We then prove consistency of the conditional mean function and show that the excess mean squared prediction error (MSPE) relative to the oracle prediction error converges to zero. We conduct simulation studies to examine nonlinear fixed-effect recovery, random-effect estimation, predictor and conditional mean estimation, and excess prediction error under different numbers of subjects and repeated observations. We also apply GNMM to a longitudinal schizophrenia dataset to predict continuous and binary depression outcomes using smartphone- based behavioral measurements and compare its predictive performance with generalized linear mixed models and conventional artificial neural networks. Both the theoretical and empirical results demonstrate that GNMM provides a flexible framework for modeling nonlinear longitudinal and clustered data. These findings provide a statistical foundation for GNMM prediction and support future methodological developments.
item.dc:creator: Mahmud Hasan, Md Moinul Ahsan, Mathias Nthiani Muia, Mous-Abou Hamadou, Chathurika S Abeykoon

item.title: Online Change-Point Detection in Linear Regression with Autoregressive Errors via Streaming Variational Bayes
item.description: arXiv:2610.15309v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large-scale streaming time-series regression requires methods that can detect structural changes while accounting for serially correlated errors and quantifying uncertainty about the current regime. We propose a streaming variational Bayes method for linear regression with autoregressive errors that combines online changepoint detection with sequential posterior inference. The proposed method processes observations in chronological mini-batches and uses a finite-mixture variational approximation to represent separate retention and reset configurations for the regression coefficients and innovation variance, while the autoregressive coefficients are shared across regimes and learned sequentially. This construction yields block-specific changepoint probabilities and posterior uncertainty summaries. Closed-form variational updates and mixture pruning enable scalable sequential inference without repeated full-data refits. In simulations, the proposed method maintains low empirical false-alarm rates under stable regimes, with posterior coverage improving as the sample size increases. Under repeated structural changes, it provides accurate type-specific changepoint detection, small changepoint location errors, and short detection delays relative to frequentist sequential monitoring procedures, while posterior coverage approaches nominal levels after an initial adaptation period. An application to high-frequency Bitcoin volatility data illustrates distinct adaptation of the regression and innovation-variance components while accounting for residual autoregressive dependence.
item.dc:creator: Yujin Jeong, Chaeeun Park, Sihyeon Pyeon, Seonghyun Jeong, Taeyoung Park

item.title: Deep Neural Mixed Models for Nonlinear Longitudinal Prediction with Subject-Specific Heterogeneity
item.description: arXiv:2610.15323v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Longitudinal health data often exhibit within-subject correlation, subject-specific heterogeneity, and complex nonlinear predictor--response relationships that may not be adequately captured by conventional mixed models. We propose a Deep Generalized Neural Network Mixed Model (DGNMM) that extends the GLMM framework by using a deep neural network to learn nonlinear population-level relationships while incorporating directly trainable, regularized subject-specific effects to capture individual heterogeneity. The model is estimated using prediction-oriented stochastic optimization with separate regularization of the neural-network parameters and subject-specific effects. This formulation allows us to investigate when increased nonlinear representation capacity provides additional predictive benefit in the presence of subject-specific heterogeneity. A simulation study varies population-level nonlinearity and subject-specific heterogeneity and compares DGNMM with GLMM, artificial neural network (ANN), Maity--Pal (MP), and GNMM alternatives for continuous and binary longitudinal outcomes. In the real-data application, DGNMM achieved the lowest MSPE for continuous depression and anxiety prediction, while alternative models remained competitive for binary outcomes. Exploratory subject-level analyses showed heterogeneous predictive gains across individuals, but the magnitude of the estimated subject-specific effects was not significantly associated with predictive gain. Overall, increased nonlinear representation capacity was most beneficial for continuous prediction under nonlinear response structures, while greater subject-specific heterogeneity did not systematically yield larger predictive gains.
item.dc:creator: Mahmud Hasan, Niloofar Ramezani, Hrishikesh Chakraborty

item.title: Identifying and Measuring Treatment-Effect Heterogeneity across Sites through Within-Site Randomization
item.description: arXiv:2610.15531v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Parallel cluster-randomized trials can identify mean effects by site characteristics and risk differences between fixed predictors, while leaving residual heterogeneity and absolute prediction risk (mean squared error of site-effect predictions) unidentified. We acquire missing same-site cross-arm information by randomizing participants within selected sites. Under randomized site selection with compatible participant reference distributions and intervention versions, we characterize necessary and sufficient observation patterns for quadratic targets in a model with unrestricted joint distributions of site response means. From finite independent participant samples, we construct unbiased moments and exact covariances. Under regularity conditions, we prove consistency as informative paired site counts grow, allowing fixed within-site sample sizes. For a fixed predictor, we optimize paired-site selection and unequal cell counts using corrected risk variances, pilot error, and costs. In an International Stroke Trial information-deletion experiment, pilot allocation reduces the conditional variance of reconstructing the complete-information corrected risk estimate by 34.3\% relative to uniform allocation with equal expected cost. In 40 Honduras villages, correction reduces estimated residual variation from 0.04081 to 0.00282 in squared log-consumption units for the same fixed explanatory basis; the explained share rises despite a smaller explained component, illustrating how participant sampling noise can inflate estimated residual variation.
item.dc:creator: Takahiro Hoshino

item.title: One Goodness-of-Fit Test Is Not Enough: Error-Controlled Localization of Misfit in Logistic Risk Models
item.description: arXiv:2610.15649v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: A goodness-of-fit test tells whether a logistic risk model fits, but the analyst also needs to know what is wrong: an overall risk that is too high is repaired by updating the intercept, risks that are too extreme by recalibration, a curved relation between score and risk by a flexible recalibration, and misfit within groups of patients only by revising the model. We split any misfit into these four parts, which are orthogonal and match the calibration hierarchy. Each part gets a group of score tests that sees that part only, and the failing parts are named by closed testing. In external validation, in large samples and for small departures, a part is wrongly named with probability at most the chosen level, and the highest part named points to the lightest update that removes the misfit. Checking a model on its development data never sees an error in the overall risk or the calibration slope, and with binary or skewed covariates it can mistake misfit within patient groups for a curved link. External validation sees all four parts, for any prediction model. In simulations it kept its error rate when the model was right and for small departures, and usually pointed to the right update. On intensive-care data its verdicts for one model differed in-sample, on similar patients and after transport.
item.dc:creator: Ebrahim Khaled Ebrahim, Ahmed El-Kotory, Osama Abd El-Aziz Hussein

item.title: Small area learning
item.description: arXiv:2610.15953v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Small area estimation (SAE) traditionally borrows strength across domains through a prespecified working model. We introduce small area learning (SAL), a learner-agnostic framework that formulates SAE as a multi-target semi-supervised learning problem and treats outcome prediction as a nuisance task. Areas may differ through unrestricted covariate shift and structured conditional shift, with information shared through common and area-specific components. We develop standard and cross-fitted estimators for low-complexity and flexible learners, unifying synthetic, model-based, and fully residual-corrected estimation. For area means, we establish consistency and asymptotic normality and provide variance estimators and confidence intervals. We extend the theory to settings with only aggregated population covariates and characterize the resulting aggregation bias. SAL reveals a bias--variance trade-off: partial residual correction can reduce mean squared error, whereas full correction yields estimators robust to working-model misspecification, potentially at higher variance. Simulations yield RMSE reductions of 34\%--49\% relative to direct estimation, with the best configuration varying across settings. An empirical application favours a cross-fitted estimator using a flexible learner under the chosen validation criterion. The numerical studies also illustrate how shrinkage can produce overly optimistic confidence intervals at the expense of strong modeling assumptions.
item.dc:creator: Katarzyna Reluga, Nicola Salvati, Setareh Ranjbar, Nikos Tzavidis, Mark van der Laan

item.title: When Treatments Spill Over: A Neural Framework for Spatiotemporal Causal Effect Estimation
item.description: arXiv:2610.16086v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Real-world public health policies are often enacted by local jurisdictions, but their effects can ripple through connected populations. For causal evaluation, this creates a difficult spatiotemporal problem: intermittent policy updates create path-level treatments, and because spillover depends on neighboring treatment paths along with the focal-unit's own history, controlling time-varying confounding requires high-dimensional, multimodal information from both sources. To address this challenge, we develop a neural spatiotemporal spillover framework that extends potential-outcome causal analysis to networked policy-systems with unit-level effects and structured interference. The framework indexes each unit's potential outcomes through own-treatment and neighborhood spillover-exposure paths, yielding direct, spillover, and total effects. We introduce an LSTM-based representation-learning encoder that integrates each unit's own and neighborhood histories into compact sequential summaries for downstream modeling and causal estimation. These summaries feed a self-normalized kernel inverse-probability-weighting estimator for continuous spillover exposure. Beyond theoretical guarantees, simulations show improved performance over outcome-regression baselines; in a practically motivated county-level COVID-19 policy study, the framework finds both business-and-economic restrictions and education-and-childcare policies associated with lower subsequent case burden, with larger estimates for business-and-economic restrictions. Overall, it provides a scalable, policy-interpretable framework for evaluating unit-level effects in high-dimensional, multimodal spatiotemporal systems when interventions spill over across space and time.
item.dc:creator: Shaohui Zhang, Jiasheng Shi, Jing Huang

item.title: When Sample-Splitting Choices Matter in TMLE and AIPW: Cross-Fitting, Targeting, and Repetition
item.description: arXiv:2610.16192v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Variants of targeted maximum likelihood estimation (TMLE) and augmented inverse-probability weighting (AIPW) with machine-learning nuisance models differ in which observations train them, how bias is corrected, and whether splits are repeated. In known-truth simulations of a binary-outcome average treatment effect, eight headline estimators shared each setting's library, inner folds and truncation bound; coverage differences were judged against a prespecified two-percentage-point margin. With a low-complexity library and good overlap (n = 3000), all but a half-sample baseline covered equivalently (0.928-0.939). With one random forest on the primary data-generating mechanism, estimators fitting the propensity in-sample undercovered severely (0.12-0.48), whereas cross-fitting both nuisances raised coverage to 0.91-1.00, two overcovering. Under near-positivity, every AIPW estimator covered better than every TMLE estimator with the unweighted fluctuation (0.907-0.917 versus 0.656-0.806 at the primary setting, all undercovering); looser truncation widened the gap. At the primary settings, pooled-versus-fold-specific and single-versus-double cross-fit constructions (involving four additional estimators) were usually equivalent; under extreme weights, pooled-targeting estimates were 1.7-1.8 times as dispersed as fold-specific ones. Repetition reduced partition dependence but made several intervals more conservative. Two real-data analyses illustrate these sensitivities. Results support cross-fitting both nuisances when empirical-process conditions cannot be justified, and assessing truncation and AIPW-versus-TMLE sensitivity under poor overlap.
item.dc:creator: M. Ehsan Karim, Rainie Fu

item.title: Enhancing Statistical-Computational Balance in Uncertainty Quantification of Bagging: A Cheap Bootstrap Approach
item.description: arXiv:2610.16243v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Bagging, which refers to the repeated subsampling of data and averaging the resulting outputs, is a common approach to reduce sampling variability of unstable learning and data-driven optimization procedures. However, uncertainty quantification for these bagged estimators, namely to generate confidence intervals for their target quantities, faces challenges in the simultaneous attainment of coverage validity while being computationally affordable. The latter refers to the practical consideration of overall resampling effort which, when using conventional bootstraps for instance, would lead to nested resampling procedures and thus can be multiplicatively large. In this paper, we develop an interval construction approach that is both asymptotically coverage-valid and computationally light in that it does not use much more than the resampling effort in the bagging scheme itself. Our approach builds on the recent so-called cheap bootstrap idea, a method designed to substantially reduce the number of resamples based on an integrative treatment between data noises and Monte Carlo resampling noises, and an in-depth derivation of the algorithmic configurations under which the Monte Carlo error from incomplete bagging is negligible. Our theory shows that our required computation budget is significantly smaller than existing methods in relation to the bag size and number of Monte Carlo subsamples. Numerical experiments in random forests, as well as an optimality bound estimation in stochastic optimization where bagging is useful, show that our proposed intervals achieve reliable coverage with low computation cost.
item.dc:creator: Arindam RoyChowdhury, Henry Lam

item.title: Honest Inference for High-Dimensional Linear Models
item.description: arXiv:2610.16503v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We propose a heteroskedasticity-robust and dimention-adaptive test for multiple linear restric- tions in sparse high-dimensional linear regression models. It combines desparsified LASSO estimation with a ridge-regularized quadratic form statistic and critical values that adapt to the restriction dimension. Under stated regularity conditions, our approach is asymptotically valid under a fixed or diverging number of restrictions without specifying the asymptotic regime in advance. Our random-design theory allows independent non-identically distributed covari- ate rows with marginal sub-Weibull tails and heteroskedastic errors satisfying finite polynomial moments. Monte Carlo simulations demonstrate improved finite-sample size control relative to conventional Wald tests, particularly as the number of restrictions increases.
item.dc:creator: Dennis Lim, Pengjin Min, Jonathan H. W. Tan, Jiezheng Wei

item.title: Quickest Change-point Detection in Generalized Linear Models with Variational Estimation
item.description: arXiv:2610.16616v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We consider quickest change-point detection in generalized linear models when the post-change parameter is unknown. Such problems arise, for example, when monitoring whether the relationship between a learned representation and an observed response changes over time. Since detection must occur soon after a change, the post-change parameter must be estimated from a limited number of observations, making finite-sample estimation accuracy particularly important. We propose a window-limited CUSUM procedure that estimates the post-change parameter using a variational-inequality (VI) formulation. For noncanonical links, VI estimation can offer favorable finite-sample accuracy over short windows despite the asymptotic efficiency advantage of maximum likelihood estimation. We characterize how estimation error reduces the effective post-change information rate and affects detection delay, and derive finite-window guarantees accounting for both statistical error and incomplete numerical optimization. The resulting procedure retains false-alarm control and achieves first-order asymptotic optimality under suitable conditions. Numerical experiments compare detection delay and update cost for fixed-budget estimation and benchmark VI-WLCUSUM against alternative detectors.
item.dc:creator: Jonghyeok Lee, Yao Xie

item.title: Bounding MrP: Subnational public opinion estimation without detailed census data
item.description: arXiv:2610.16726v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Multilevel regression with post-stratification (MrP) is the dominant method for estimating public opinion in subnational units. The method requires the full joint distribution of demographic variables in a subnational unit, which is often unavailable from public census tabulations. Existing approaches fill this gap by imposing assumptions to combine marginal distributions of census variables into a synthetic joint distribution. We propose sharp MrP bounds instead: the smallest interval containing all estimates of subnational public opinion consistent with the marginal distributions alone. The bounds solve a pair of linear programs and are computationally feasible for typical applications in political science. Applied to two prominent examples in the literature, the bounds are tight enough to be informative and often more accurate than MrP restricted to a coarser, observed joint distribution of census variables. The bounds serve as margin-consistent interval estimates and a diagnostic when researchers use a synthetic joint distribution to construct MrP estimates.
item.dc:creator: Moritz Marbach

item.title: Adaptive Cauchy inference from invariant information
item.description: arXiv:2610.16789v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Selecting weights and projection directions from the observations used for testing can invalidate a reference distribution. We develop a framework for exact conditional inference under rotation symmetry. A maximal invariant permits adaptation while leaving a uniform common phase for calibration. This yields explicit Cauchy references for invariantly selected weights and projections. Under separate block rotations, the same principle gives exact normal-score combinations with coefficients selected from all blockwise invariants. The calibration results require neither densities nor moments. To illustrate the framework, we study direction learning and power in spherical Gaussian location models, identifying a regime in which consistent detection is possible without consistent direction recovery. For heterogeneous functional data, a matched mean--residual construction produces the required null symmetry under a conditional Gaussian model. Simulations compare Radius and Blend, two representative procedures, with sample splitting, and an electrocardiogram analysis illustrates their application.
item.dc:creator: Yiming Liu, Shaochen Wang

item.title: An Integrated Framework for Rule-Based Data Editing
item.description: arXiv:2610.16947v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This paper develops a mathematical framework connecting structural metadata, logical admissibility, and correction in statistical data editing. A normalized routing graph generates a canonical indexed representation and an associated Horn theory, incorporating explicit semantic edits through deterministically evaluated auxiliary variables. Under specified record semantics, the theory characterizes admissibility, distinguishes structural minimality from logical irredundancy, and permits validation without materializing the deductive closure. Canonical indices preserve the provenance and dependency scopes of violations. With complete diagnostics and strictly positive weights, a nonnegative violation Hamiltonian vanishes exactly on admissible corrections within the permitted candidate domain. Verified zero-energy outputs therefore certify feasibility and global minimization of violation energy. Minimum modification cost is formulated separately, with sufficient conditions for an equivalent penalized objective and optimality certificates obtained by matching attained costs with valid lower bounds. A household survey application verifies admissible corrections and certifies minimum cost for a subset of returned records through a retrospective audit. The framework connects structural requirements to correction certificates independently of the numerical search procedure, while statistical accuracy of replacement values requires separate assessment.
item.dc:creator: Pierpaolo Massoli

item.title: Implicit and explicit reparameterizations of the Folded Normal and Rice distributions
item.description: arXiv:2610.17151v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Variational inference is a flexible tool for modeling experimental data and has proven useful in crystallography. Pathwise gradient estimators provide low-variance gradients for reparameterized variational inference, but are not readily available for some distributions central to crystallography. This work derives and implements implicit and explicit reparameterized gradient estimators for the folded Normal and Rice distributions in \prog{PyTorch}, and compares their variance analytically and empirically. In each case the implicit estimator achieves lower variance for the location derivative, particularly at small location-to-scale ratios, while the scale-derivative variances are nearly equal. For both distributions, implicit estimator is proved to be the conditional expectation of the explicit estimator given the sampled magnitude, so its variance is never larger. As a practical application, French-Wilson scaling is formulated as a variational inference problem, using the folded Normal and Rice distributions as variational families for centric and acentric reflections, respectively. Both estimators recover the exact posterior to better than $1\%$ on the amplitude, and converge at the same rate. The implementations are available in the open-source package \prog{rs-distributions}.
item.dc:creator: Luis Aldama, Kevin Dalton, Minhuan Li, Doeke Hekstra

item.title: Frequentist and Bayesian population pharmacometrics: similarities, differences, and practical implications
item.description: arXiv:2610.17340v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Although the frequentist versus Bayesian debate has a long-standing history, and both are well-established approaches for inference, they are often considered separately in pharmacometric literature, with their theoretical and practical differences receiving limited direct comparison. We address this gap by providing a conceptual background and comparative evaluation of frequentist and Bayesian methods for parameter inference in pharmacometrics. First, we highlight the theoretical and algorithmic differences between approaches within a general and pharmacometric context. We then apply both to classical compartmental pharmacokinetic models using simulated and real data; initially through evaluating four inference methods (two frequentist, two Bayesian) across a range of simulated data conditions, followed by investigating each inference approach in the practical setting. The simulation studies facilitate evaluation of the sensitivity of the methods to sample size, number of observations, residual noise and inter-individual variability, comparing the performance with respect to relative error, confidence/credible interval coverage and bias in the estimated variability. The real-world data analysis further highlights how each approach quantifies and presents uncertainty estimates by examining this for both the parameter estimates and system dynamics. By providing a theoretical and practical comparison that highlights the similarities and differences between approaches, this work aims to lower the barrier to understanding and implementing Bayesian and frequentist inference in pharmacometrics.
item.dc:creator: Jodie A. Cochrane, Haini Wen, Liang Yang, Tyler Cassidy, Sara Hamis

item.title: Selective Inference for Clustering Under Unknown Covariance
item.description: arXiv:2610.17458v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Unsupervised clustering is widely used to discover underlying group structure, after which researchers often seek to validate these groups via post-hoc hypothesis testing on the population means. However, using the same data both to form clusters and to test for a difference in means inflates the Type I error rate. Recent work in selective inference has proposed solutions when the underlying data are drawn from a multivariate Gaussian distribution with a known covariance matrix or an unknown isotropic covariance matrix. We propose a new selective test for the difference in means between two clusters that provably controls the Type I error rate under an arbitrary unknown covariance matrix. Our test statistic does not require estimating the feature covariance matrix; instead, it leverages a Monte Carlo sampling procedure over the set of orthogonal matrices. We show that this new selective test can be computed efficiently, and we derive closed-form solutions when clusters are formed using k-means or hierarchical clustering. In simulations, we demonstrate that our proposed p-value controls the selective Type I error rate and achieves substantial power, and we illustrate its application on gene expression and drug review data sets.
item.dc:creator: Yiqun T. Chen, Lucy L. Gao

item.title: The Geographic Moran Effect: Theory, Methods, and Interpretation
item.description: arXiv:2610.17497v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The Moran effect traditionally refers to the synchronization of population dynamics driven by shared environmental forcing rather than direct interactions among populations. Although extensively studied in ecology, the Moran effect has received limited attention in geography, and its applicability has yet to be fully explored. In this study, we build upon the classical Moran effect in population ecology as a conceptual foundation, developing a more comprehensive conceptual framework in a geographic context. We introduce the new concept Geographic Moran Effect (GME), defined as temporally coherent and synchronized variation across geographic entities induced by common external forcing, with the magnitude and potentially the direction of local responses varying according to a spatially varying sensitivity field. A two-step spatiotemporal factor framework is developed to identify and interpret the GME. The framework first tests for the possible presence of GME-type synchrony in spatiotemporal data and then examines the GME and its spatiotemporal evolution by investigating its structure through spatial and temporal dimensions separately. A synthetic experiment validates the framework's reliability, while an application to U.S. county-level presidential election data (2008-2024) demonstrates its ability to identify the GME and its spatial and temporal components. By redefining the Moran effect as a geographic theory and a distinct object of inference, this work provides a mechanism-oriented perspective on spatiotemporal analysis with broad applicability in geography, ecology, and public health, where explicitly identifying and interpreting GME-type synchrony is essential for understanding system-level dynamics.
item.dc:creator: Zhenzhi Jiao, X. Angela Yao, Jean-Claude Thill

item.title: E-Backtesting Expected Shortfall without Value-at-Risk Forecasts under Time-series Models
item.description: arXiv:2610.17681v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Expected Shortfall (ES) measures the average size of tail losses. Its sequential backtests typically also require a Value-at-Risk (VaR) forecast. We develop two e-backtesting methods using only observed losses and ES forecasts: one for iid losses only and the other for time series under an AR-GARCH conditional VaR structure. Under the stated assumptions, both control false rejections at any stopping time. For the time-series method, validity requires a fixed parameter--quantile pair representing the conditional VaR path and a positive report margin. The time-series statistic takes an infimum over possible parameter and VaR values. We choose the betting process $(\lambda_t)$ by maximizing an empirical growth rate averaged across candidate parameters. We compute the statistic by continuous VaR profiling on a dense parameter grid. For grid approximations, we prove convergence to the continuous infimum, together with convergence of the probability of false rejection, as the grid is refined over a fixed monitoring period. Lower and upper bounds for the VaR infimum on the parameter grid control the accuracy of the numerical profiling. Simulations, including ES reports that change from over-reporting to under-reporting, and an application to daily NASDAQ losses provide numerical comparisons with VaR--ES e-processes and fixed-sample ES backtests, assessing detection frequencies and the timing of rejections.
item.dc:creator: Ruodu Wang, Jingcheng Yu

item.title: Linear Regression Beyond Covariance: Latent Slope Spectra from Higher-Order Cumulants
item.description: arXiv:2610.17772v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Least squares summarizes the joint distribution of a response and regressor through second-order information. When an observed regressor is composed of latent components carrying different relationships with the response, this summary can average over distinct linear effects. We study the additional linear information contained in higher-order mixed cumulants and formalize it through the latent slope spectrum. Ordinary least squares is a variance-weighted barycenter of this spectrum, whereas higher-order cumulants can separate its components when the spectrum is sufficiently parsimonious. In the scalar one-confounder model, fourth-order cumulants identify the unordered pair $\{\beta,\beta+\gamma\}$ through a $2\times2$ linear system and a quadratic equation. We develop estimation and root-$n$ inference under regular separation and show that detection and estimation diverge near degeneracy: slope multiplicity remains detectable on an $n^{-1/4}$ local scale even when the individual slopes are not uniformly regularly estimable. In multiple regression, a quadratic tensor recurrence yields a test of one versus multiple effective coefficient vectors that does not require the vectors themselves to be identified; multiplicity can therefore be consistently detectable even when the recurrence operator is noninjective. The same quadratic diagnostic can retain signal in directions where a first-order higher-cumulant restriction cancels exactly. The results distinguish representation, identification, detection, and estimation of latent linear heterogeneity, while making explicit the limits of structural and causal interpretation from observational data alone.
item.dc:creator: Anirban Nath, Ming Yuan

item.title: Spatial Kernel Restricted Canonical Correlation Analysis: Population Targets, Identifiability, and Stability
item.description: arXiv:2610.17830v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Relating observations of different categories across space requires methods that accommodate distinct sampling locations and spatial dependence. Spatial kernel restricted canonical correlation analysis (skrCCA) uses spatial weights to identify associated feature combinations across data categories. Here, we develop a statistical theory of its covariance form after feature reduction. Conditional on the observed locations and under a mean-zero model, the pairwise association matrices target kernel-weighted averages of cross-covariances. For prespecified directions, we derive the exact null variance under independence between blocks. We establish recovery and stability bounds in two- and multiblock settings under explicit population models, and show that exact cyclic updates have convergent objective values. The variance characterization shows how spatial weighting and within-block dependence jointly determine the effective information available for estimating association. The recovery bounds separate statistical and optimization error, relating stability to population separation and the strength of connections between blocks. These results clarify what fitted spatial association axes estimate and provide conditions under which they can be recovered reliably.
item.dc:creator: Zhen Miao, Yilong Qu, Nancy R. Zhang

item.title: Free-support Wasserstein Resampling in Sequential Monte Carlo
item.description: arXiv:2610.17924v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In modern sequential Monte Carlo (SMC) applications, such as diffusion model samplers, propagating a particle is expensive, so only a few particles can be afforded. In this regime, each resampling step decides which regions of the state space survive, so a better resampling scheme is worth extra computation. However, classical resampling methods only replicate existing particles and suffer from sample impoverishment, especially when the particle size is small relative to the dimension. To create new particles, we relax the unbiasedness of resampling and control the mean squared error via a Wasserstein criterion. Specifically, we propose Wasserstein-Dirichlet resampling (WDR), which constructs an equal-weight measure that optimally approximates the weighted particle distribution by solving a free-support Wasserstein barycenter problem. We then randomize the resulting optimal coupling by Dirichlet mixing. Theoretically, we provide non-asymptotic mean squared error bounds that quantify the bias-variance trade-off and show that the rate depends on the intrinsic dimension. A truncated variant preserves high-weight particles while applying WDR to the remaining mass, targeting mild weight degeneracy. Experiments on state-space models and conditional image generation demonstrate that WDR consistently improves estimation accuracy, stability, and sample diversity. The improvements persist at matched wall-clock cost when the propagation cost dominates.
item.dc:creator: Mengyu Li, Cheng Meng, Jun S. Liu

item.title: ndscape: a structural map of the nested dichotomy space
item.description: arXiv:2610.18050v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Nested dichotomies (NDs) reduce multiclass classification to a tree of binary classifiers. Tree structure can change accuracy, bias, and variance, but the full space of structures has not been mapped in aggregate. We introduce ndscape, a two-dimensional mapping of ND structures based on depth-weighted structural tokens. We use this embedding to conduct what is, to our knowledge, the first bias-variance analysis across the ND structure space. In simulations with 6 to 10 classes, NDs with similar tree structures exhibit similar squared bias, variance, and squared probability loss, regardless of whether the binary classifier is logistic regression or a decision tree. Variance, however, follows mean root-to-leaf depth when logistic regression is used at each node, so flatter, more balanced NDs are more stable, whereas with decision-tree node models, variance is not associated with depth and differs little across ND structures. On six datasets with 6 to 19 classes, held-out accuracy, log loss, and prediction variance remain spatially organised on the same topology-only map. None of the six standard construction heuristics tested selects a tree from the best-performing cluster on any dataset, although some select high-performing individual trees. The ndscape embedding turns ND selection from one opaque construction step into a readable comparison of class groupings, exposing the upper-level splits that distinguish high-performing and stable regions.
item.dc:creator: Maxwell Dix-Matthews, Melinda Hodkiewicz, Adriano Polpo

item.title: Rational Quadratic Kriging
item.description: arXiv:2610.18077v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This article proposes rational quadratic kriging, a kriging estimator that addresses the limitations of existing approaches: the mean reversion issue of ordinary kriging and the diverging variance issue of rational kriging. Through the rational quadratic kernel, we establish a connection between rational quadratic kriging and kernel regression. The connection allows us to prove desirable theoretical properties of the new estimator and further propose a novel estimation procedure that utilizes factor weights from kernel regression. We also derive expressions to enable efficient leave-one-out estimation and conformal prediction. Extensive simulations across both deterministic functions and noisy datasets show significant improvements in both prediction and uncertainty quantification. A fast implementation is available in the open-source R package RQK.
item.dc:creator: Difan Song, V. Roshan Joseph

item.title: Sparse-group Convoluted Smoothed Quantile Regression in High Dimension
item.description: arXiv:2610.18232v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In many applications, covariates are naturally organized into groups, yet conventional group-selection methods often retain all variables within selected groups, failing to achieve within-group sparsity. To address this limitation, we propose an adaptive two-stage sparse-group selection procedure for high-dimensional quantile regression. The proposed method integrates convolution-smoothed quantile loss with $\ell_{2,0}$ and $\ell_0$ penalties to identify important groups and relevant variables within them, achieving sparsity at both levels. We establish theoretical guarantees for sure screening and exact support recovery at both stages, as well as consistent model-size selection using information criteria, with explicit bounds on failure probabilities. The proposed procedure is computationally efficient by restricting optimization to selected groups and active variables. Simulation studies and a breast cancer gene-expression analysis demonstrate its competitive performance in variable selection, estimation accuracy, and computational efficiency, while identifying biologically relevant genes and delivering accurate quantile predictions.
item.dc:creator: Jing Lv, Anxi Wang

item.title: Residual Model Criticism for Fitted SDE Implementations
item.description: arXiv:2610.18271v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Stochastic differential equation (SDE) models can reproduce trajectories while missing temporal dependence. We compare residual-based scores from a held-out path with scores from paths simulated by a fitted implementation, keeping fitted parameters, simulation rules and the scoring rule fixed. We give conditions for Monte Carlo calibration and bound conditional rejection error by the gap between conditional score CDFs. Residuals use zero-noise centres and covariance approximations that track noise propagation over observation intervals; report residuals also include reporting variation. Residual weights affect sensitivity and the influence of fitting error. For a quadratic energy score in a linear example with singular true covariance, whitening with nonsingular fitted covariance matrices leaves a nonvanishing score-CDF gap as nonzero coefficient estimates approach the truth. A fixed positive-definite weighting matrix makes the gap vanish.
