In a controlled SIR experiment using reference paths simulated at fitted parameters, adding susceptible-state endpoints to training or downweighting a low-variance residual reduces null rejection. A separate comparison using reference paths simulated at the true parameter shows reduced sensitivity to added susceptible-coordinate noise after downweighting. An exploratory weekly-report application incorporates reporting and reconstruction into reference simulations, revealing excess correlation between squared residuals in Czechia and persistently negative residuals in Finland.
item.dc:creator: Shengda Zheng

item.title: Multilevel Main Effects Matrix Factor Model
item.description: arXiv:2610.18335v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We propose a multilevel main effects matrix factor model (MMEFM) to extract meaningful row and column effects from groups of matrix data. As a generalization of a multilevel matrix factor model, we provide rigorous definitions of MMEFM and identifications, together with iterative algorithms for the estimators of all global and local components in the main effects and common component, including global/local main effects and core ranks, with rates of convergence spelt out. An important feature of the model is that all main effects can be nonstationary and still be consistently estimated at each time point. At the same time, our estimated global common factors are alignment independent, and hence are truly global, and can be presented and given interpretations more easily. We propose a Bootstrap procedure for detecting the existence and identifying the groups of data that are driven by the global common factors. The power of the test, together with the accuracy of various estimators, are demonstrated in extensive simulation settings. Estimation performance is also compared to other state-of-the-art methods for matrix time series by simulations and a set of U.S. equity data. All numerical works are done using the R package MMEFM, which is available at CRAN.
item.dc:creator: Kaixin Liu, Clifford Lam, Zetai Cen

item.title: Simultaneous Inference for Centre-Outward Rankings of Random Objects
item.description: arXiv:2610.18533v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In many applications one object is chosen to represent a sample and the least typical objects are set aside, usually without any measure of uncertainty. We measure how central an object is by its reference depth, the probability that a random reference point is closer to it than to a random opponent. Using only pairwise dissimilarities, we construct simultaneous intervals for all ranks, a centre set that contains the most central observation under stated conditions, and outlier sets that contain only objects among the least central ones, each with asymptotic probability at least a prescribed level. These guarantees hold even though the ranked objects are themselves random. For symmetric distributions on the real line, the centre set has the smallest possible order of size up to a logarithmic factor, and in dimension three or more it reduces to the most central observation with probability tending to one. For typical meteorological years the centre set usually contains several candidate years, so the data do not determine the year on which building-energy simulations rest; for three collections of gene trees it contains one tree, whose features can be reported as those of the most central tree.
item.dc:creator: Lingfeng Lyu, Doudou Zhou

item.title: From Fourier Amplitudes to Persistence Images for Impact-Echo Defect Detection
item.description: arXiv:2610.18732v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Impact-echo testing is a nondestructive testing method used to detect internal defects in concrete structures. However, boundary reflections, structured interference, and measurement noise can produce complex Fourier amplitude spectra, making defect classification difficult. We constructed a two-dimensional frequency--amplitude persistence image (FA-PI) from the Fourier amplitude spectrum. Using a fixed parameterization of exact multi-parameter persistent homology, each retained Fourier component is represented with frequency-bin location as one coordinate and amplitude as the other, and Gaussian kernels are then applied in this two-dimensional space. This construction has a direct analytical connection to the corresponding one-dimensional Gaussian-smoothed Fourier amplitude spectrum. FA-PI was evaluated on an experimental backfill-void dataset and a public bridge-deck impact-echo dataset, and compared with raw and Gaussian-smoothed Fourier amplitude spectra using a linear classifier with a Softmax output and identical signal-level data splits. The evaluation included original signals and signals corrupted by Gaussian noise, sinusoidal interference, or mixed noise, with matching noise types and signal-to-noise ratios during training, validation, and testing. Performance was assessed using accuracy and macro-averaged precision, recall, and F1-score. Across the two datasets, FA-PI consistently outperformed the raw and Gaussian-smoothed Fourier baselines in the noisy-condition summaries. These findings indicate that representing Fourier spectral components in a two-dimensional frequency--amplitude space can improve impact-echo defect classification beyond frequency-axis smoothing alone.
item.dc:creator: Keunsu Kim, Suyoung Choi, Meiyan Kang

item.title: Designing for Prediction: Planning Formulas for Expected Out-of-Sample $R^2$ and $r$
item.description: arXiv:2610.18781v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Design calculations let researchers gauge, before data is collected, whether a planned study is likely to detect an effect. In this paper, we develop such calculations for predictive models using ordinary least squares and ridge regression under leave-one-out cross-validation. To do so, we derive closed-form expressions relating the expected out-of-sample $R^2$ and the expected correlation between observed and predicted outcomes to four design-stage quantities: sample size, number of predictors, an assumed population $R^2$ ($\rho^2_{in}$) and a design efficiency factor $D^*$ (which summarizes how leverage is distributed across observations). Unlike the classical shrinkage formulas, which depend only on sample size and dimension, these are sensitive to how covariates are arranged -- to imbalance and skew. A simulation study assesses the accuracy of the formulas against realized values under a variety of data generating mechanisms. We apply the methods to a published study predicting personality from smartphone behavior and show that the design formulas would have indicated, before any analyses were run, that least squares could not be expected to beat the sample mean while ridge could. An R package, predpower, implements the calculations.
item.dc:creator: Elizabeth Tipton

item.title: Open-ended Scientific Discovery with Possibilistic Reasoning
item.description: arXiv:2610.11289v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Autonomous scientific discovery with LLMs requires generating and testing hypotheses adaptively as evidence accumulates while maintaining statistical validity. Existing anytime-valid methods can handle data-dependent hypotheses, but open-ended discovery poses a deeper challenge: the best discovered hypothesis may still be the best of a bad lot, with better explanations yet undiscovered, while even background knowledge such as physical laws may require revision in light of new findings. In response, we formalize the problem as Abductive Autonomous Scientific Discovery (AASD) using possibility theory. We introduce abductive utility, a computable measure of discovery progress, and possibility frontier search, the first algorithm for AASD, which maintains anytime validity and achieves $\varepsilon$-optimal abductive utility asymptotically under suitable conditions. Experiments on synthetic and real-world scientific-discovery tasks show strong performance.
item.dc:creator: Anita Yang, Siu Lun Chau, Tomoya Wakayama, Krikamol Muandet, Masaki Adachi

item.title: SIRNET: Causal Adaptation of Pretrained Embeddings for Semiparametric Treatment-Effect Estimation Under Surrogacy
item.description: arXiv:2610.14011v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Modern experiments increasingly produce rich post-treatment objects---such as text, images, and video---that may provide early surrogate signals for outcomes that are delayed, expensive, or observed only for a subset of participants. A pretrained encoder can turn such an object into a strong generic embedding, but the embedding is not trained for the estimation tasks required by a causal estimator and may emphasize information irrelevant to the causal target. We propose SIRNET, a Surrogate-Informed Representation adaptation framework for neural-NETwork-based causal estimation in the presence of unstructured post-treatment surrogates. Starting from pretrained surrogate embeddings, SIRNET learns a shared adapter jointly for outcome prediction, treatment propensity, and arm-specific surrogate marginalization, beyond the generic pretraining objective. The resulting covariate and surrogate representations provide a common interface for these nuisance tasks. The final treatment-effect estimate and confidence interval are obtained from cross-fitted orthogonal scores that attain the semiparametric efficiency bound under the stated nuisance-rate conditions. We also validate SIRNET's performance in synthetic and semisynthetic experiments, as well as the Anti-Amyloid in Asymptomatic Alzheimer's Disease (A4) trial, using frozen pretrained brain-MRI embeddings as surrogates for a long-term outcome.
item.dc:creator: Lei Shi, Qiuran Lyu

item.title: Bayesian Uncertainty Quantification of Breast-Cancer Pathology AI Agreement under Reader- and Annotation-Condition-Dependent Reference Labels
item.description: arXiv:2610.14642v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Human reference labels used to evaluate medical AI can vary across readers and annotation workflows. We quantified agreement of a fixed pathology AI system with a future qualified reader without treating inferred consensus as error-free biological truth. Linked Evaluation and Unbiased NuCLS multirater data were analyzed using a fixed external HoVer-Net decision vector. The selected frame contained 1,144 anchors, 52 fields of view, five slides/patients, and five primary readers. The target was fixed-AI agreement with a future reader, with descriptive contrast $\Delta=\theta_E-\theta_U$. Analyses included raw agreement and iMRMC benchmarks, reader-only and shared-detectability Bayesian models, structural sensitivities, adversarial simulations, and predictive assessment. Among 5,188 reader-anchor pairs observed in both conditions, 19.62% changed AI-agreement state, while raw agreement was 0.5466 in Unbiased and 0.5473 in Evaluation. The reader-only model gave $\Delta=-0.0008$ (95% CrI, $-0.0033$ to $0.0008$), and the shared-detectability model gave $\Delta\approx0$ ($-0.0140$ to $0.0127$). Across structural perturbations, absolute agreement ranged from 0.420 to 0.646 in Unbiased and 0.409 to 0.640 in Evaluation. Frozen adversarial simulations met the comparative-stability criterion (median $R=0.295$; 14/16 model-scenario cells had $R<1$). Held-out-AI prediction supported shared predictive information, but varied by slide composition. The Evaluation-minus-Unbiased contrast was comparatively stable, whereas absolute agreement was structurally sensitive. These findings do not establish equivalence, causal assistance effects, biological accuracy, or new-patient transportability. Evaluations using variable human references should report reader population, selected frame, observation mechanism, and structural sensitivity.
item.dc:creator: Hammed A. Olayinka

item.title: Recurrent Barycenter Encoder: Prediction, Simulation and Applications to Time Series Analysis
item.description: arXiv:2610.15027v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: This dissertation has two parts. In the first part we theoretically develop a framework that extends the optimal transport barycenter problem from independent data with observed covariates to processes whose relevant covariate is their own history. Given a stationary stochastic process, our framework shows there exists an invertible transport map that extracts from it an iid component whose distribution is the barycenter of the conditional distributions of the input process on its own past. This extracted iid sequence thus captures the innovation or noise component of the process that is not explained by the process's own past. In the second part of this thesis we implement an effective algorithm to solve this problem and test it against synthetic data generated with some well-known models in time series analysis for which the solution is known in closed-form. We then show how this method can be applied to build a predictive sampler for such processes, and assess the accuracy of this predictive sampler both with the aforementioned synthetic data and with real-world time series such as the S&P 500 and Bitcoin 4-hour returns, and the daily records of the North Atlantic Oscillation index from the NOAA Physical Sciences Laboratory. Finally, we demonstrate an application of the sampler to path simulation with a well-known time series model.
item.dc:creator: Javier I Almarza

item.title: A model-assisted design for phase I oncology drug combination trials incorporating backfill
item.description: arXiv:2610.15065v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Historically, phase I oncology trials were designed with the focus to find the highest tolerable dose. However, given the FDA's acknowledgment that the highest tolerable dose might not be the dose which is optimal biologically, there is an increased emphasis the development of designs that explore the dose-toxicity and dose-efficacy relationship. Backfill designs have emerged as a popular response to address this need by allocating participants to doses deemed safe while awaiting participants outcomes. Previous designs have explored how to assign participants to doses in backfill designs in a rigorous manner while providing simplicity and performance (a class of designs known as model-assisted) for single agents. Still, a research gap exists in the lack of model-assisted backfill designs for drug combinations. Frequently, the combinations two of cancer agents are explored in phase I trials, with the goal of identifying the highest tolerable combination. This paper incorporates and extends methodology based on previous model-assisted backfill designs to provide clinicians with a simple-to-use backfill design for phase I drug combination trials.
item.dc:creator: Connor Celum (Statistics Department, California Polytechnic State University, San Luis Obispo, USA), Evan M. Bagley (Department of Public Health Sciences, Medical University of South Carolina, Charleston, USA, Hollings Cancer Center, Medical University of South Carolina, Charleston, USA)

item.title: Energy-Guided Learning for Heat Equation with Noisy Source: Optimal Estimation and Generalization Bounds
item.description: arXiv:2610.15111v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Data and the governing partial differential equations (PDEs) of continuous-time dynamical systems provide rich structure for statistical learning. A central challenge is how to integrate data with PDE constraints in a principled way to improve generalization. In this paper, we characterize the statistical estimation and generalization properties of learning solutions to the heat equation with a noisy source function from finite, randomly sampled data. We first derive a novel variational formulation, which we characterize as the minimizer of loss function for an energy regularized and ellipticity debiased Sobolev regression. By formulating the learning task as a supervised problem over space-time domains under physically meaningful norms, our approach goes beyond the traditional supervised learning framework by effectively leveraging \emph{auxiliary data}---samples of the source function of the heat equation---to design a \emph{physics-informed energy regularization}. Our analysis reveals that learning in linear parabolic PDEs exhibits intrinsic anisotropy between spatial and temporal regularity, in sharp contrast to the static elliptic problems, leading to fundamentally different estimation and generalization behaviors. Specifically, we derive non-asymptotically rate-optimal estimation errors, as well as generalization error, which explicitly capture the interplay among temporal sampling, spatial resolution, and solution smoothness. Our numerical experiments demonstrate substantial orders of magnitude of reduction in testing errors against various physics-informed neural network methods on various parabolic and hyperbolic PDEs.
item.dc:creator: Zixiang Zhou, Xiaohui Chen, Shanghua Teng

item.title: Rank-based Model Average Estimator for Average Treatment Effects
item.description: arXiv:2610.15553v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Model averaging emerges as an attractive ensemble technique that strategically synthesizes all available information from potential candidate models to enhance estimation accuracy. Despite of having been widely practiced in various areas in biostatistics and economics, its application to causal inference is rather limited. We propose to estimate the average treatment effect (ATE) by forming the weighted combination of the robust rank-based estimators obtained from a series of candidate models, where the model weights, selected via the growing window cross-validation, dynamically adjust the importance of candidate models. The proposed robust rank-based model averaging ({\sf RRMA}) is not only robust to handle potential outliers and heavy-tailed error distributions but also capable to reduce the risk of model mis-specification and enhance the flexibility and the accuracy of estimation. Theoretically, we establish the desirable asymptotic properties of {\sf RRMA}, including the asymptotic optimality, consistency and asymptotic distribution. Moreover, motivated by the asymptotic distribution of {\sf RRMA}, an easy-to-implement confidence interval is also developed for the ATE. Simulation experiments and an empirical application demonstrate the superiority of {\sf RRMA} over existing competitors in estimation accuracy, coverage probabilities and widths of confidence intervals.
item.dc:creator: Jing Lv, Jialiang Li

item.title: Adaptive Robust Confidence Sets in High Dimensions
item.description: arXiv:2610.15723v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We study adaptive confidence sets for mean vectors of multivariate Gaussians with identity covariance under Huber contamination when the contamination proportion is unknown. We show that an information-theoretically optimal adaptive confidence set can be constructed by simultaneously quantifying uncertainty across all one-dimensional projections. The resulting confidence set achieves the optimal diameter and reveals a substantial adaptation cost compared with the minimax estimation error. Although statistically optimal, this construction is computationally infeasible. We establish a Statistical Query (SQ) lower bound showing that achieving diameter $O(m^{-1/2})$ requires either exponentially many queries or query tolerance $d^{-\Omega(m)}$. Thus, in contrast to robust mean estimation, adaptation to the unknown contamination proportion incurs both a statistical cost and a computational barrier within the SQ framework. Finally, we give a low-degree moment-matching algorithm that constructs an adaptive confidence set using $d^{O(m)}$ samples and time. Its diameter bound contains an additional $O(m^{-1/2})$ term beyond the information-theoretic rate, matching the dependence on $m$ in the SQ lower bound. Together, these results characterize the statistical limits of adaptive robust confidence sets under Huber contamination and quantify a computational barrier within the SQ framework.
item.dc:creator: Ilias Diakonikolas, Chao Gao, Daniel M. Kane, Yuetian Luo

item.title: Jensen-Bregman split Gibbs sampling
item.description: arXiv:2610.15853v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Split Gibbs sampling (SGS) is a versatile tool to sample from complex posterior distributions, such as those arising in imaging inverse problems. However, existing SGS instances are limited to quadratic variable couplings, restricting their applicability to Gaussian likelihoods. This letter genearalizes SGS to non-Euclidean geometry by introducing a coupling kernel defined through a Jensen-Bregman divergence. This framework not only enables posterior sampling in these settings but also unifies several \emph{ad hoc} sampling schemes from the literature under a principled theoretical foundation.
item.dc:creator: Nicolas Dobigeon, Mame Diarra Fall, Eric Barat

item.title: Fisher Information and Differentiability for $r$-Largest Generalized Extreme-Value Models
item.description: arXiv:2610.16136v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: The $r$ largest observations of a block form a dependent random vector whose support moves with all three parameters of the $r$-largest generalized extreme-value ($r$GEV) model. For a fixed number $r$ of order statistics, we show that the model is differentiable in quadratic mean if and only if $k_0<1/2$, where $k=-\gamma$ is the shape parameter; the threshold is thus the same as for block maxima, because only the largest or the smallest retained order statistic can reach the moving boundary. In this range the Fisher information is positive definite and decomposes into the block-maximum information plus contributions of the lower order statistics, and it equals the negative expected Hessian, which we prove without using any estimator. The model is then locally asymptotically normal, whereas for $k_0\ge1/2$ root-$n$ local asymptotic normality fails. Numerically, using the five largest order statistics instead of the block maximum alone lowers the efficient asymptotic standard error by about $45\%$ for the shape parameter and by $20$--$24\%$ for the 100-year return level in heavy-tailed cases ($k_0\le-0.2$), but by only about $2\%$ for the return level when $k_0=0.4$.
item.dc:creator: Jihong Park, Yire Shin, Jeong-Soo Park

item.title: Distributional Regression for Arbitrary Response Variables Using ReLU Neural Networks
item.description: arXiv:2610.16142v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: This paper develops a unified framework for distributional regression with arbitrary response variables. Rather than relying on scalar thresholds or Euclidean structure, we model conditional event probabilities indexed by measurable sets, which extends distributional regression to general response spaces while retaining a direct connection to classical event-based formulations. Within this framework, we study two complementary estimators: a preliminary estimator based on separate regression of event indicators, and a constrained estimator that enforces inclusion-consistent predictions through a directed acyclic graph (DAG) over a finite set family. We establish general error bounds for both estimators and further specialize the results to dense ReLU networks, yielding explicit convergence rates overcoming the curse of dimensionality. Simulation studies and real-data experiments further demonstrate the practical effectiveness of the proposed framework.
item.dc:creator: Junpeng Ren, Carlos Misael Madrid Padilla, Oscar Hernan Madrid Padilla

item.title: Online Individualized Treatment Selection under Partial Feedback: False Discovery Control and Minimax Optimality
item.description: arXiv:2610.16464v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We study online individualized treatment selection when only the outcome under the assigned treatment is observed. Our objective is to preferentially treat individuals whose potential outcomes under treatment exceed a covariate-specific control reference, while limiting false discoveries among treated individuals. We propose Partial-Feedback Adaptive Individualized Treatment Selection (PAITS), which initializes learning from historical data and combines sequential estimation of local null risks, randomized exploration, and feedback-driven updates of the treatment selection threshold. Under regularity conditions, we establish asymptotic false discovery rate control and sublinear gap-weighted assignment regret relative to a population oracle. We further establish a minimax lower bound on assignment regret under prescribed uniform nuisance-estimation requirements and give conditions under which PAITS attains the corresponding constrained minimax rate up to logarithmic factors. These results quantify the tradeoff between accurate treatment assignment and nuisance learning under partial feedback. Simulation studies and a real-data analysis using the Jester recommendation dataset illustrate the finite-sample performance of PAITS.
item.dc:creator: Runzhe Gu, Zinan Zhao, Wenguang Sun, Xintao Xia

item.title: Locally adaptive step sizes for Hamiltonian Monte Carlo methods
item.description: arXiv:2610.16506v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Exact reversible locally adaptive step sizes are introduced by Bou-Rabee et al. (2026) in the context of the No-U-Turn Hamiltonian Monte Carlo (HMC) sampler for the purpose of high performance HMC sampling in challenging target distributions. This paper carefully explains and illustrates the locally adaptive step size procedure under more general assumptions. Alternative error measures are introduced with the aim of further enhancing MCMC performance by reducing the prevalence of reversibility failure rejections. In addition, the paper shows how to introduce the locally adaptive step sizes also within standard HMC and Metropolis-corrected kinetic Langevin/generalized HMC (GHMC). Finally, a numerical study of the relative merits of the proposed error measures in the context of different Hamiltonian flow-based MCMC methods is provided.
item.dc:creator: Jimmy Huy Tran, Tore Selland Kleppe, Nawaf Bou-Rabee

item.title: A Composite Bayesian Risk--Distributionally Robust Optimization Model for Stochastic Programming with Elliptical Distribution Ambiguity
item.description: arXiv:2610.16883v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We study a stochastic optimization problem in which the random vector follows a semiparametric elliptical distribution with unknown location and shape parameters and an unspecified radial distribution. Assuming that the decision maker only has access to samples of the random vector, we develop a framework to jointly address parameter uncertainty and distributional ambiguity arising from this composite structure. To update the posterior distribution of the parameters, a key challenge is that the density of an elliptical distribution depends on the unknown radial distribution, and hence conventional likelihood-based Bayesian inference is infeasible. To overcome this challenge, we propose a novel estimating-equation-based Gibbs inference framework that updates posterior distributions of model parameters solely through estimating equations. For elliptical distributions, we construct a pair of estimating equations for the location and shape parameters that are invariant to the radial component, which enables posterior learning without specifying the density. For the distributional uncertainty, we construct an ambiguity set for the radial distribution by transforming observed samples into pseudo-samples of the radial variable. Combining the above components, we formulate a composite Bayesian risk--distributionally robust optimization model, in which the inner problem captures worst-case radial distributions within the ambiguity set, and the outer problem evaluates the decision risk induced by the parameter uncertainty through a user-specified risk measure. We further develop a cutting-plane algorithm to solve the resulting optimization problem. Numerical experiments demonstrate that the proposed approach provides substantial performance improvements over benchmark methods, including sample average approximation and distributionally robust optimization.
item.dc:creator: Renjie Chen, Huifu Xu

item.title: Measuring Variable Importance Using Proportional Inclusive Marginal Effects
item.description: arXiv:2610.17053v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Shapley-based measures are widely used for measuring variable importance in statistics and machine learning. However, these measures have a serious issue--a nonactive variable can get a positive importance measure when it is correlated with an active variable. Herin et al. recently proposed a measure called proportional marginal effects (PME) that mitigates this spurious effect. However, PME is developed for deterministic models and has high computational cost. In this article, we propose a new measure called proportional inclusive marginal effects (PRIME) that overcomes these two limitations of PME. The key idea in PRIME is to use a novel model-free variable selection technique to identify the active variables and include only them in the computation of the importance measure. Analysis of test functions and real datasets show that PRIME can accurately and reliably quantify variable importance from noisy input-output data.
item.dc:creator: Youngseo Cho, V. Roshan Joseph

item.title: Beyond the Kullback--Leibler divergence: the likelihood-ratio distribution as a detectability measure
item.description: arXiv:2610.17186v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: The Kullback--Leibler (KL) divergence is the expectation value of the log-likelihood ratio between two specified models, evaluated with respect to one of the two models. It provides an average measure of the distinguishability of the models. We examine its connection to discovery potential and the accuracy of parameter estimates when one model represents a null hypothesis, and the alternative is a family of models characterized by one or more continuous parameters. For data drawn from a multivariate Gaussian distribution, we derive the log-likelihood-ratio distribution and its cumulants under two such hypotheses. We then search over the alternative model's parameter space and use peak prominence, the height of a likelihood-profile peak above its surrounding baseline, as an operational detection statistic. Repeating this search on simulated data drawn from the null model allows us to calibrate the prominence threshold for a specified false-positive rate. We study a toy Gaussian model as well as three cosmological examples involving cosmic topology, the tensor-to-scalar ratio, and dark energy. In all these cases, detectability of a particular model depends not only on KL divergence, but also on the size of the model parameter space, the likelihood-ratio distributions, and the distance of the model from any parameter space boundaries. The relationship between KL divergence, discovery potential, and parameter estimation must therefore be calibrated for each family of models and detection statistic under consideration.

Starkman (COMPACT Collaboration), Cynthia Trendafilova (COMPACT Collaboration), Yashar Akrami (COMPACT Collaboration), Stefano Anselmi (COMPACT Collaboration), Javier Carr\'on Duque (COMPACT Collaboration), Craig J. Rodrigues (COMPACT Collaboration), Andrius Tamosiunas (COMPACT Collaboration)

item.title: Overlap, Not Moments: Finite-Sample Theory for Bridge Sampling
item.description: arXiv:2610.17403v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Bridge sampling estimates of marginal likelihoods are routinely reported with a delta-method Monte Carlo standard error (MCSE). Existing theory is asymptotic and cannot say whether a given run is long enough to trust the estimate or its MCSE. We give finite-sample answers. The optimal bridge estimator fits a logistic regression that separates posterior from proposal draws, and its accuracy is governed by their overlap, within a factor of two of the classification's Bayes error. Because the estimating function is a sum of bounded terms, no moment conditions are needed, and all bounds hold uniformly over targets, proposals and dimensions. A number of draws inversely proportional to the overlap suffices and is necessary in the worst case, paralleling the exponential-in-Kullback--Leibler requirement of importance sampling. A Berry--Esseen bound with an explicit constant holds at the optimal rate, and the MCSE is accurate once the effective overlap is large; it is estimated at no cost. For Markov chain draws, the required sample size grows in proportion to the sampler's relaxation time, unavoidably in the worst case. The estimated bridge, the fixed-point iteration and the fitted proposal matter only at second order, and we give free diagnostics for sampler failure and misestimated autocorrelation.
item.dc:creator: Giorgio Micaletto

item.title: The hypervariational method: a general, automated technique based on innovations to tune the parameters of the Hybrid covariance matrix
item.description: arXiv:2610.17561v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: The Hybrid forecast covariance model is an operationally successful way to build a background error covariance matrix. It is constructed as a weighted sum, with scalar weights, of the climatological covariance matrix and a localized ensemble covariance matrix, with a localization matrix typically depending on a localization length. For best performance, the Hybrid needs to be optimized by tuning those weights and, possibly, other parameters, such as the localization length. Here, a systematic and automated method for this tuning operation is introduced. This technique is referred to as hypervariational method, and it is formulated in terms of a cost function, built using a time series of innovations as an essential ingredient. This cost function, which depends on the parameters, is minimized when they have optimal values. Equations for its minimization, based on Newton's method, are derived. Besides the aforementioned, commonly used Hybrid, the hypervariational method is applicable to any known Hybrid (and to any set of parameters on which it depends analytically), including recently developed Hybrids, not necessarily constructed as weighted sums. Here, the hypervariational method is applied to tune the ensemble covariance matrix weight in the seminal-formulation Hybrid (which does not feature localization). This is done in a synthetic experimental setting where a theoretically-derived expression for the optimal value for that weight is known. Moreover, in that experimental setting, a further method, based on a linear fit procedure, to determine that optimal value is possible. Both the hypervariational method and that linear fit procedure are shown to produce an optimal weight value matching (up to a tolerance of $0.1$) the optimal value known from the theory. Furthermore, Newton's minimization in the hypervariational method is shown to converge immediately (at the first recursive step).
item.dc:creator: Francesco Sardelli (School of Geography, Earth and Atmospheric Sciences, University of Melbourne, Australia), Craig H. Bishop (School of Geography, Earth and Atmospheric Sciences, University of Melbourne, Australia, Bureau of Meteorology, Australia)

item.title: textGrain watermarking is harder to detect: can sum-tests still do it optimally?
item.description: arXiv:2610.17655v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Watermarking embeds an imperceptible signal in text from large language models that is statistically detectable with a secret key. The recent textGrain watermark (Li et. al. (2026b)) calibrates this signal against the model's sampling entropy through an explicit entropy budget, combining the stochasticity of Red-Green and the unbiasedness of Gumbel-max watermarks, and its accompanying report proposes a detector that sums pivotal statistics. We study when, and how efficiently, textGrain can be detected after human edits, modeled as a sparse mixture in which a fraction $\varepsilon_n\asymp n^{-p}$ of positions retain the watermark and token uncertainty decays as $n^{-q}$. First, entropy calibration comes at a cost: the minimax detection boundary of textGrain is $p+q=1/2$, so its detectable region is strictly smaller than that of Gumbel-max and maximal-coupling watermarks, whose boundary is $2p+q=1$. This cost stems from textGrain's construction rather than from entropy calibration itself: an unbiased scheme with the same entropy loss remains detectable where textGrain is not. Second, perhaps surprisingly, this loss makes the sum detector optimal at the boundary when the number of transport columns is fixed, unlike for Gumbel-max. When the number of columns grows and the entropy budget does not vanish, the detectable region expands while that of the sum detector does not. Third, for a fixed edit fraction, we characterize the optimal exponential rate of type II error decay and show that the sum detector falls strictly short of it at every fixed alternative. Finally, we propose a weighted multiscale binomial scan, valid in finite samples and needing no knowledge of the next-token distributions, entropy budget, or edit fraction; it attains every detection boundary above and the optimal exponent.
item.dc:creator: Swapnaneel Bhattacharyya, Soham Bonnerjee

item.title: How to Train Your Intercept: A Comparison of Intercept Update Strategies in Coordinate Descent
item.description: arXiv:2610.18043v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Coordinate descent solvers for regularized generalized linear models (GLMs) differ in how they update the intercept. This seemingly routine choice can substantially affect convergence when the response is imbalanced. For direct coordinate descent on the original GLM loss, we compare a conservative step based on worst-case curvature, a safeguarded Newton step based on current curvature, and repeated Newton steps that solve the intercept subproblem. The conservative update can leave much of the interaction between the intercept and the coefficients unresolved, producing a slowdown when that interaction controls convergence. A single Newton step avoids this attenuation and, in our experiments, follows nearly the same outer trajectory as exact minimization while requiring fewer inner steps. Simulated and real-data experiments, including comparisons across six production solvers and a controlled intervention within skglm, support this explanation. We also show how the same mechanism appears in quadratic-approximation methods and extends to multinomial models with rare classes. We recommend a safeguarded Newton update for direct coordinate descent and full intercept optimization within frozen local quadratic surrogates.
item.dc:creator: Johan Larsson, Frederik Fabricius-Bjerre

item.title: A new approach for estimating the number of spikes in high-dimensional Gaussian models
item.description: arXiv:2610.18059v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: In this paper, we study the estimation of the signal subspace dimension $k$ in a $p$-variate signal-plus-noise complex Gaussian model, when the noise covariance matrix is assumed to be diagonal or Toeplitz. We consider the high-dimensional asymptotic regime in which both the data dimension $p$ and the available sample size $n$ diverge to infinity at the same rate, while we also allow $k$ to diverge at a slower speed. In this context, the classical estimates of the literature, consistent in the high-dimensional regime, often rely on the a priori knowledge of an upper bound $k_*$ of $k$, which can be misspecified in practice. Our proposed approach relies on building estimates of the tracial moments of the noise covariance matrix using the $p-k_*$ smallest eigenvalues of the sample covariance matrix (SCM), which are in turn used to build a threshold above which the $k$ largest eigenvalues are isolated. The resulting estimate of $k$ is proved to be consistent in the high-dimensional regime, even for the misspecified situations where $k_* < k$. Numerical experiments in different challenging scenarios illustrate the improvement of the proposed approach over the aforementioned methods.
item.dc:creator: Hugo Jeannin, Pascal Vallet, Florent Bouchard, Guillaume Ginolhac, Audrey Giremus

item.title: Interpolation and coherence in multiple testing
item.description: arXiv:2610.18205v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: In the literature on multiple testing methods that control the familywise error rate, a fundamental concept is "coherence". A procedure is coherent if it is "logically consistent" (Hochberg and Tamhane, 1987) in the sense that if a hypothesis is rejected, then all hypotheses that imply it are also rejected. If a method is not coherent, then it can be made coherent without increasing the familywise error rate. Recently, the concept of coherence was generalized to a much broader class of multiple testing procedures, namely all methods that provide simultaneous confidence bounds for false discovery proportions. Such procedures were defined to be coherent if they cannot be further improved through a process called "interpolation". However, we show that such a coherent procedure can sometimes be further improved by exploiting remaining logical inconsistencies. This leads to what we call a "perfectly coherent" method. Thus, interpolation does not necessarily lead to perfect coherence. However, we provide conditions under which it does. Fortunately, many methods based on interpolation turn out to be perfectly coherent.
item.dc:creator: Ninh Tran, Dennis Leung, Jesse Hemerik

item.title: Strategic Multi-Agent Resource Allocation via Statistical Contracts
item.description: arXiv:2610.18336v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We study a class of strategic hypothesis testing problems in which a principal aims to allocate resources among competing agents who possess data or data-generating mechanisms that may be relevant to the principal's goals. Each agent can pay a participation cost to opt into a statistical contract, in which case they generate data from a private distribution and receive an allocation based on a predetermined (and publicly known) mechanism. Each agent is either "null" or "non-null" and the principal's goal is to design the contract to limit the allocation to the former while maximizing transactions with the latter. Using e-values, we define a "continuous-closure," a set of allocations which prevents null agents from profiting in expectation and provides post-hoc risk control for general loss functions under arbitrary dependence. When the loss is the fraction of resources allocated to null agents, the region admits polynomial-time linear optimization. We also give explicit, interpretable closed-form approximations, and we analyze participation from a non-null agent's perspective, giving conditions under which entry into the contract is profitable. Finally, we extend the framework to support online arrival of the agents, in which case the principal has to make irrevocable on-the-fly decisions, and provide a method which gives time-uniform error-control in this setting.
item.dc:creator: Ben Chugg, Michael I. Jordan, Aaditya Ramdas

item.title: Risk Measures for the Climate Transition Age: Why Symmetric Risk Budgets are unlikely to mitigate two-dimensionally asymmetric Climate Change risks
item.description: arXiv:2610.18387v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: The most widely used investment risk measures - variance, standard deviation, and tracking error - treat upside deviations as equally undesirable as downside losses. In stable markets with assumed symmetric return distributions, this simplification is potentially harmless. In the climate transition age, it is not. Climate risk is two-dimensionally asymmetric, across assets and over time. Both dimensions are negatively skewed against investors. Hence, climate transition investment strategies deliberately deviate from benchmarks that reflect an insufficiently decarbonising global economy. When fiduciaries enforce tracking error budgets that penalise outperformance just as heavily as underperformance, they inadvertently constrain exactly the portfolio return opportunities that climate-aware investing seeks. We argue that replacing symmetric deviation-based risk measures with their downside-only counterparts - semi-variance, standard risk and trailing error - resolves this conflict without sacrificing any fiduciary discipline. The distinction is not merely semantic: as the gap between climate transition trajectories and market benchmarks widens over the coming decades, symmetric risk budgets will become binding constraints on transition strategies well before actual investment risk warrants it. We propose specific changes to mandate design that would allow institutional investors to pursue climate transition opportunities within genuinely risk-aware (rather than deviation-averse) frameworks.
item.dc:creator: Lars Dijkstra, Andreas G. F. Hoepner, Fabiola I. Schneider, Agnieszka S{\l}omka-Go{\l}\k{e}biowska

item.title: How Low Can You Go: Fine-Tuning LLMs with Bayesian Optimization (LlMBO)
item.description: arXiv:2610.18504v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Recently, Morris et al. introduced TinyLoRA, a strategy for LLM fine-tuning which introduces arbitrarily few parameters, and demonstrated accuracy improvements using less than $10$ parameters rather than the ${\gtrsim 10,000}$ typically demanded by LoRA-based methods. However, that study continued to use gradient-based local search methods of the kind deployed for training multi-billion parameter LLMs in the first place. This article is predicated on the observation that, in the low dimensional setting, global optimization methods become tractable, unlocking Large language Model Bayesian Optimization (LlMBO). LlMBO is sample-efficient, gradient-free, memory-light, parallelizes across devices without synchronization, and, unlike policy-gradient methods, can optimize greedy-decoding accuracy directly. We describe numerical experiments comparing LlMBO against GRPO on fine-tuning tasks for a variety of models on a math benchmark suite which show that LlMBO can be a suitable alternative in this regime, matching or exceeding GRPO's fine tuning gains, while using a fraction of the compute and memory.
item.dc:creator: Aditya Kulkarni, Davide Sartor, Carlos Soto, Nathan Wycoff

item.title: Inference for Fr\'echet Mean Sets
item.description: arXiv:2610.18646v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We construct confidence sets for the entire Fr\'echet mean set by inverting studentized pairwise risk inequalities. Gaussian multiplier calibration localized around empirical near minimizers gives asymptotic coverage at least the nominal level, uniformly over distribution classes satisfying empirical-process conditions. The construction requires neither unique ness nor a manifold structure. We characterize the limiting binding directions and give conditions for exact asymptotic coverage. On the intrinsic circle, exactness holds for every fixed non-point-mass law and uniformly over a family in which two means merge at a quar tic minimum. With ideal multiplier quantiles, the construction reproduces the Euclidean Wald set under both nonsingular and singular covariance. Under regular local conditions, it is first-order equivalent to intrinsic Wald inference.
item.dc:creator: Ryunosuke Miyazaki

item.title: Information-Enriched Selection of Stationary and Non-Stationary Autoregressions using the Adaptive Lasso
item.description: arXiv:2402.16580v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We propose a novel approach to elicit the weight of a potentially non-stationary regressor in the consistent and oracle-efficient estimation of autoregressive models using the adaptive Lasso. The enhanced weight builds on a statistic that exploits distinct orders in probability of the OLS estimator in time series regressions when the degree of integration differs. We provide theoretical results on the benefit of our approach for detecting stationarity when a tuning criterion selects the $\ell_1$ penalty parameter. Monte Carlo evidence shows that our proposal is superior to using OLS-based weights, as suggested by Kock [Econom. Theory, 32, 2016, 243-259]. We apply the modified estimator to model selection for German inflation rates after the introduction of the Euro. The results indicate that energy commodity price inflation and headline inflation are best described by stationary autoregressions.
item.dc:creator: Thilo Reinschl\"ussel, Martin C. Arnold

item.title: Inference for Heterogeneous Graphical Models using Doubly High-Dimensional Linear-Mixed Models
item.description: arXiv:2403.10034v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Inferring the structure of population-level functional connectivity networks from multi-subject functional magnetic resonance imaging data is essential for understanding the connectivity patterns underlying cognitive and behavioral functions. Graphical models provide a formal statistical framework for inferring the graph structure. However, the multi-level nature of functional magnetic resonance imaging data---where each level corresponds, for instance, to a subject---compromises the inferential validity of most existing methods. In this paper, we develop a valid inference framework for high-dimensional graphical models that accounts for cross-level heterogeneity. We introduce a neighborhood-based method to learn the graph structure and reframe the problem as that of inferring fixed effect parameters in a doubly high-dimensional linear mixed model. We then propose a LASSO-based estimator and a de-biased LASSO-based inference framework for these fixed effect parameters. We evaluate the performance of the proposed framework using benchmark simulation studies and apply it to descriptively compare graph structures between the functional connectivity networks of two predefined groups of subjects from the Human Connectome Project.
item.dc:creator: Kun Yue, Eardi Lila, Ali Shojaie

item.title: Direction Preferring Confidence Intervals
item.description: arXiv:2404.00319v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Confidence intervals (CIs) are fundamental in statistical analysis, providing interval estimates for unknown parameters. We introduce direction-preferring CIs that prioritize inference for parameters with a specific sign (e.g., positive sign). Unlike previous methods of constructing CIs, our intervals are based on the inversion of acceptance regions that differ for positive and negative parameters, to enhance the probability of determining the sign in the prespecified preferred direction while maintaining standard coverage. We apply our suggestion in the typical context that multiple parameters are considered, but only some of the constructed CIs are of interest, e.g., when CIs are reported only for the subset of parameters that are found to differ significantly from zero. This leads us to suggest direction-preferring CIs with false coverage rate (FCR) control, as well as conditional direction-preferring CIs that adjust for selection by conditioning on the selection event. We compare the two selection adjustment methods in theory and using numerical experiments. The procedures we develop are useful for inference on secondary outcomes in medical applications, a setting we highlight through two motivating examples.
item.dc:creator: Tzviel Frostig, Orestis A. Panagiotou, Yoav Benjamini, Ruth Heller

item.title: Adaptive Unit Root Inference in Autoregressions using the Lasso Solution Path
item.description: arXiv:2404.06205v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We show that the activation knot of a potentially non-stationary regressor on the adaptive Lasso solution path in autoregressions can be leveraged for selection-free inference about a unit root. The resulting test has asymptotic power against local alternatives in $1/T$ neighbourhoods, unlike post-selection inference methods based on consistent model selection. Exploiting the information enrichment principle devised by Reinschl\"ussel and Arnold (arXiv:2402.16580 [stat.ME]) to improve the Lasso-based selection of ADF models, we propose a composite statistic and analyse its asymptotic distribution and local power function. Monte Carlo evidence shows that the combined test dominates the comparable post-selection inference methods of Tibshirani et al. [JASA, 2016, 514, 600-620] and may surpass the power of established unit root tests against local alternatives. We apply the new tests to groundwater level time series for Germany and find evidence rejecting stochastic trends to explain observed long-term declines in mean water levels.
item.dc:creator: Martin C. Arnold, Thilo Reinschl\"ussel

item.title: Exploring Exchangeability within Permutation Inference: Implications for Statistics and Data Science Educators
item.description: arXiv:2406.07756v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Permutation tests are a powerful and flexible approach to inference via resampling. As computational methods become more ubiquitous in the statistics curriculum, use of permutation tests has become more tractable. At the heart of the permutation approach is the *exchangeability condition*, which determines the appropriate null sampling distribution. We explore the exchangeability condition in the context of permutation tests, including settings where the exchangeability condition is not tenable. Our examples include two-sample comparisons of means, clustered designs, multiple linear regression, and two-sample comparisons of correlation. The different exchangeability challenges in each example allow further exploration of the definition and importance of the exchangeability requirement for permutation testing. We believe that understanding the exchangeability condition and how it relates to the null hypothesis gives students the skills to work effectively with permutation tests in more complicated modeling settings and to further their understanding of statistical inference. We close with pedagogical recommendations for instructors who wish to incorporate permutation inference into their curriculum as a means to increase student understanding of resampling-based inference.
item.dc:creator: Johanna Hardin, Lauren Quesada, Julie Ye, Nicholas J. Horton

item.title: Bootstrap Adaptive Lasso Solution Path Unit Root Tests
item.description: arXiv:2409.07859v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We propose sieve wild bootstrap analogues to the adaptive Lasso solution path unit root tests of Arnold and Reinschl\"ussel (2024) arXiv:2404.06205 to improve finite sample properties and extend their applicability to a generalised framework, allowing for non-stationary volatility. Numerical evidence shows the bootstrap to improve the tests' precision for error processes that promote spurious rejections of the unit root null, depending on the detrending procedure. The bootstrap mitigates finite-sample size distortions and restores asymptotically valid inference when the data features time-varying unconditional variance. We apply the bootstrap tests to real residential property prices of the top six Eurozone economies and find evidence of stationarity to be period-specific, supporting the conjecture that exuberance in the housing market characterises the development of Euro-era residential property prices in the recent past.
item.dc:creator: Martin C. Arnold, Thilo Reinschl\"ussel

item.title: Simulations for estimation of random effects and overall effect in three-level meta-analysis of standardized mean differences using constant and inverse-variance weights
item.description: arXiv:2411.00795v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We consider a three-level meta-analysis of standardized mean differences. The standard method of estimation uses inverse-variance weights and REML/PL estimation of variance components for the random effects. We introduce new moment-based point and interval estimators for the two variance components and related estimators of the overall mean. Similar to traditional analysis of variance, our method is based on two conditional $Q$ statistics with effective-sample-size weights. We study, by simulation, bias and coverage of these new estimators. For comparison, we also study bias and coverage of the REML/PL-based approach as implemented in {\it rma.mv} in {\it metafor}. Our results demonstrate that the new methods are often considerably better and do not have convergence problems, which plague the standard analysis.
item.dc:creator: Elena Kulinskaya, David C. Hoaglin

item.title: WMAP: An R Package for Causal Meta-Analysis by Integrating Multiple Observational Studies
item.description: arXiv:2501.01041v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Integrating multiple observational studies for meta-analysis has sparked much interest. The presented R package WMAP (Weighted Meta-Analysis with Pseudo-Populations) (Guha et al., 2026) addresses a critical gap in the implementation of integrative weighting approaches for multiple observational studies and causal inferences about various groups of subjects, such as disease subtypes. The package features three weighting approaches, each representing a special case of the unified weighting framework introduced by Guha and Li (2024), which includes an extension of inverse probability weights for data integration settings. It performs meta-analysis on user-inputted datasets as follows: (i) it first estimates the propensity scores for study-group combinations, calculates subject balancing weights, and determines the effective sample size (ESS) for a user-specified weighting method; and (ii) it then estimates various features of multiple counterfactual group outcomes, such as group medians and differences in group means for the mRNA expression of eight genes. Additionally, bootstrap variability estimates are provided. Among the implemented weighting methods, we highlight the FLEXible, Optimized, and Realistic (FLEXOR) method, which is specifically designed to maximize the ESS within the unified framework. The use of the software is illustrated through simulations and a multi-site breast cancer case study based on a simulated dataset modeled after real TCGA data from seven medical centers.
item.dc:creator: Subharup Guha, Mengqi Xu, Chayce Reed, Kashish Priyam, Yi Li

item.title: Targeted Data Fusion for Region-Specific Survival Effects in the AMP HIV Prevention Trials
item.description: arXiv:2501.18798v5 Announce Type: replace Abstract: The Antibody Mediated Prevention (AMP) trials opened a new scientific frontier by showing that passively administered monoclonal broadly neutralizing antibodies (bnAbs) could prevent HIV-1 acquisition. The trials enrolled 4,611 participants across four epidemiologically distinct regions, with 174 HIV-1 diagnoses observed during follow-up. Regional heterogeneity in treatment efficacy, together with privacy and regulatory limits on central data pooling, calls for methods that borrow strength across regions without sharing individual-level data. To estimate region- and treatment-specific survival curves under distributional heterogeneity, we develop a federated learning approach that combines site-specific estimators via an L1-regularized criterion that downweights data sources not aligned with the target. We further extend the framework to a general class of causal contrasts, including the survival difference, survival ratio, and restricted mean survival time difference. In the AMP analysis, for example, the standard error of the day-148 survival difference decreased from 0.007 using the target-only estimator to 0.004 using the federated estimator. For women in South Africa, the region-specific analyses provided no strong evidence of an overall VRC01 benefit, consistent with the primary AMP findings. Overall, the proposed approach provides region-adaptive inference with improved precision without sharing individual-level data, while preserving estimation of region-specific treatment effects under cross-region heterogeneity.
item.dc:creator: Yi Liu, Alexander W. Levis, Ke Zhu, Shu Yang, Peter B. Gilbert, Larry Han

item.title: Bayesian local clustering of functional data via semi-Markovian random partitions
item.description: arXiv:2503.08881v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We introduce a Bayesian framework for indirect local clustering of functional data, leveraging B-spline basis expansions and a novel dependent random partition model. By exploiting the local support properties of B-splines, our approach allows partially coincident functional behaviors, achieved when shared basis coefficients span sufficiently contiguous regions. This is accomplished through a cutting-edge dependent random partition model that enforces semi-Markovian dependence across a sequence of partitions. By matching the degree of the B-spline basis with the semi-Markovian dependence structure, the proposed model serves as a highly flexible prior, enabling efficient modeling of localized features in functional data. Furthermore, we extend the utility of the dependent random partition model beyond functional data, demonstrating its applicability to a broad class of problems where sequences of dependent partitions are central, and standard Markovian assumptions prove overly restrictive. Empirical illustrations, including analyses of simulated data and tide level measurements from the Venice Lagoon, showcase the effectiveness and versatility of the proposed methodology.
item.dc:creator: Giovanni Toto, Antonio Canale

item.title: A longitudinal Bayesian framework for estimating causal dose-response relationships
item.description: arXiv:2505.20893v5 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Existing causal methods for time-varying exposure and time-varying confounding focus on estimating the average causal effect of a time-varying binary treatment on an end-of-study outcome, offering limited tools for characterizing marginal causal dose-response relationships under continuous exposures. We propose a scalable, nonparametric Bayesian framework for estimating marginal longitudinal causal dose-response functions with repeated outcome measurements. Our approach targets the average potential outcome at any fixed dose level and accommodates time-varying confounding through the generalized propensity score. The proposed approach embeds a Dirichlet process specification within a generalized estimating equations structure, capturing temporal correlation while making minimal assumptions about the functional form of the continuous exposure. We apply the proposed methods to monthly metro ridership and COVID-19 case data from major international cities, identifying causal relationships and the dose-response patterns between higher ridership and increased case counts.
item.dc:creator: Yu Luo, Kuan Liu, Ramandeep Singh, Daniel J. Graham

item.title: Dependent Dirichlet processes via thinning
item.description: arXiv:2506.18223v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: When analyzing data from multiple sources, it is often convenient to strike a careful balance between two goals: capturing the heterogeneity of the samples and sharing information across them. We introduce a novel framework to model a collection of samples using dependent Dirichlet processes constructed through a thinning mechanism. The proposed approach modifies the stick-breaking representation of the Dirichlet process by thinning, that is, setting equal to zero a random subset of the beta random variables used in the original construction. This results in a collection of dependent random distributions that exhibit both shared and unique atoms, with the shared ones assigned distinct weights in each distribution. The generality of the construction allows expressing a wide variety of dependence structures among the elements of the generated random vectors. Moreover, its simplicity facilitates the characterization of several theoretical properties and the derivation of efficient computational methods for posterior inference. A simulation study illustrates how a modeling approach based on the proposed process reduces uncertainty in group-specific inferences while preventing excessive borrowing of information when the data indicate it is unnecessary. This added flexibility improves the accuracy of posterior inference, outperforming related state-of-the-art models. An application to the Collaborative Perinatal Project data highlights the model's capability to estimate group-specific densities and uncover a meaningful partition of the observations, both within and across samples, providing valuable insights into the underlying data structure.
item.dc:creator: Laura D'Angelo, Bernardo Nipoti, Andrea Ongaro

item.title: Assumption-Lean Differential Variance Inference for Heterogeneous Treatment Effect Detection
item.description: arXiv:2512.03254v5 Announce Type: replace Abstract: The conditional average treatment effect (CATE) is frequently estimated in clinical studies to refute a homogeneous treatment effect hypothesis. Under this regime, all patients making up the population experience identical benefit from a given treatment relative to a comparator. Uncovering heterogeneous treatment effects through inference about the CATE, however, requires that covariates truly modifying the treatment effect be reliably collected at baseline. CATE-based techniques will necessarily fail to detect violations when effect modifiers are omitted from the data due to, for example, resource constraints. Severe measurement error has a similar impact. Clinical decision makers can be misled as a result. To address these limitations, we prove that a practical homogeneous treatment effect hypothesis can be gauged through inference about contrasts of the potential outcomes' variances even when effect modifiers are missing from the data. We derive causal machine learning estimators of these contrasts and study their asymptotic properties. We establish that these estimators are doubly robust and asymptotically linear under mild conditions, permitting formal hypothesis testing about treatment effect heterogeneity. Numerical experiments demonstrate that these estimators' asymptotic guarantees are approximately achieved in finite-sample randomized and observational study data alike. These inference procedures are then used to detect heterogeneous treatment effects in the re-analysis of randomized controlled trials investigating targeted temperature management in cardiac arrest patients.
item.dc:creator: Philippe A. Boileau, Hani Zaki, Gabriele Lileikyte, Niklas Nielsen, Patrick R. Lawler, Mireille E. Schnitzer

item.title: Detecting Impact of the Great Recession on Macroeconomic Indicators
item.description: arXiv:2512.04444v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We study structural changes in multivariate time series by estimating and comparing stationary graphs of macroeconomic time series before and after an economic crisis, such as the Great Recession. Building on a latent time series framework called Orthogonally-rotated Univariate Time-series (OUT), we propose a shared-parameter framework-the spOUT autoregressive model (spOUTAR)-that jointly models two related multivariate time series and enables coherent Bayesian estimation of their corresponding stationary precision matrices. This framework provides a principled mechanism for detecting and quantifying which conditional relationships among the variables changed or formed following the crisis. Specifically, we study the impact of the Great Recession (December 2007-June 2009) that substantially disrupted global and national economies, prompting long-lasting shifts in macroeconomic indicators and their interrelationships. While many studies document its economic consequences, less is known about how the underlying conditional dependency structure among economic variables changed as economies moved from pre-crisis stability through the shock and back to normalcy. Using the proposed approach to analyze U.S. and OECD macroeconomic data, we demonstrate that spOUTAR effectively captures recession-induced changes in stationary graphical structure, offering a flexible and interpretable tool for studying structural shifts in economic systems.
item.dc:creator: Shuvrarghya Ghosh, Arkaprava Roy, Anindya Roy, Subhashis Ghosal

item.title: Fully Bayesian Spectral Clustering and Benchmarking with Uncertainty Quantification for Small Area Estimation
item.description: arXiv:2512.15643v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: In this work, inspired by machine learning techniques, we propose a new Bayesian model for Small Area Estimation (SAE), the Fay-Herriot model with Spectral Clustering (FH-SC). Unlike traditional approaches, clustering in FH-SC is based on spectral clustering algorithms that utilize external covariates, rather than geographical or administrative criteria. A major advantage of the FH-SC model is its flexibility in integrating existing SAE approaches, with or without clustering random effects. To enable benchmarking, we leverage the theoretical framework of posterior projections for constrained Bayesian inference and derive closed form expressions for the new Rao-Blackwell (RB) estimators of the posterior mean under the FH-SC model. Additionally, we introduce a novel measure of uncertainty for the benchmarked estimator, the Conditional Posterior Mean Square Error (CPMSE), which is generalizable to other Bayesian SAE estimators. We conduct model-based and data-based simulation studies to evaluate the frequentist properties of the CPMSE. The proposed methodology is motivated by a real case study involving the estimation of the proportion of households with internet access in the municipalities of Colombia. Finally, we also illustrate the advantages of FH-SC over existing Bayesian and frequentist approaches through our case study.
item.dc:creator: Jairo F\'uquene-Pati\~no

item.title: Coherent Information Deletion: Bayesian, Generalized Bayesian and Possibilistic Unlearning
item.description: arXiv:2602.09061v5 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Bayes' theorem admits an information processing interpretation due to Zellner (1988): under the Shannon information criterion, the posterior is the unique rule that processes prior and data information without information loss. We revisit these ideas from the perspective of information deletion. Given a posterior based on a complete dataset, what distribution should replace it when a subset of the data is removed? For ordinary Bayesian inference, we show that the corresponding information deletion objective is uniquely minimized by the leave-data-out posterior. We then extend the framework beyond likelihood-based inference from Bayes to the generalized Bayesian updating of Bissiri et al.(2016} based on loss functions. Requiring deletion to be coherent under sequential removal of loss contributions yields a deletion rule that exactly recovers the generalized posterior based only on the retained information. We further develop an axiomatic theory, beyond probabilistic inference, for possibilistic deletion and show that the same information-deletion perspective leads to a principled rule for exact possibilistic unlearning. Finally, restricting these exact deletion principles to tractable families leads naturally to variational Bayesian, generalized Bayesian, and maxitive possibilistic unlearning.
item.dc:creator: Hans Montcho, H{\aa}vard Rue, Maurizio Filippone

item.title: Prior Smoothing for Multivariate Disease Mapping Models
item.description: arXiv:2602.10955v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: To date, we have seen the emergence of a large literature on multivariate disease mapping. That is, incidence of (or mortality from) multiple diseases is recorded at the scale of areal units where incidence (mortality) across the diseases is expected to manifest dependence. The modeling involves a hierarchical structure: a Poisson model for disease counts (conditioning on the rates) at the first stage, and a specification of a function of the rates using spatial random effects at the second stage. These random effects are specified as a prior and introduce spatial smoothing to the rate (or risk) estimates. What we see in the literature is the amount of smoothing induced under a given prior across areal units compared with the observed/empirical risks. Our contribution here extends previous research on smoothing in univariate areal data models. Specifically, for three different choices of multivariate prior, we investigate both within prior smoothing according to hyperparameters and across prior smoothing. Its benefit to the user is to illuminate the expected nature of departure from perfect fit associated with these priors, providing measures of their smoothing behavior not captured by conventional measures of predictive performance. We propose both theoretical and empirical metrics for our investigation and illustrate with both simulated and real data.
item.arxiv:journal_reference: Retegui, G., Ugarte, M. D., Etxeberria, J., & Gelfand, A. E. (2026). Prior smoothing for multivariate disease mapping models. Spatial Statistics, 76, Article 101055
item.dc:creator: Garazi Retegui, Mar\'ia Dolores Ugarte, Jaione Etxeberria, Alan E. Gelfand

item.title: Design-based theory for covariate adjustment in generalized pairwise comparisons
item.description: arXiv:2602.18383v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Generalized pairwise comparisons summarize treatment effects in randomized experiments with ordinal, multivariate, or prioritized outcomes. We study optimal covariate adjustment under complete randomization, with potential outcomes and covariates fixed and treatment assignment as the sole source of randomness. We derive the exact randomization variance of the unadjusted estimator and characterize linear calibration adjustments using the between-arm difference in covariate means. The asymptotic variance is a strictly convex quadratic in the adjustment coefficient, yielding a closed-form optimum. The resulting estimator is asymptotically no less efficient than the unadjusted estimator, with an explicit precision gain that clarifies which covariates improve precision. However, natural pair-level and single-arm least squares adjustments generally use weights that differ from the allocation-dependent optimum and can substantially reduce efficiency. We also propose a within-arm variance estimator for asymptotically conservative inference, whose conservatism arises from unidentifiable joint variation in a unit's two potential scores, and show that residualizing each arm on its own projection coefficient saves the discrepancy that governs the efficiency loss of conventional adjustments. In the special case where the comparison function is the outcome difference, our proposed covariate-adjusted estimator is first-order equivalent to the fully interacted regression adjustment of Lin (Ann. Appl. Stat., 2013, 7, 295-318).
item.dc:creator: Xinyuan Chen, Fan Li

item.title: Transportable inference using target population summary statistics under covariate shift
item.description: arXiv:2603.02474v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Transporting findings from a study population to a target population is central to evidence-based decision-making in real-world settings. Most existing methods require individual-level data from both populations to account for covariate shift. However, privacy regulations and data-sharing constraints often preclude access to such data from the target population, leaving only covariate summaries available for analysis. In this paper, we develop transportability methods that enable valid inference using source individual-level data and target covariate summaries. First, we apply entropy balancing to transportability, enabling source individual-level data to be adjusted to match the target covariate moments. We establish asymptotic normality for the entropy balancing estimator and propose a variance estimator to account for uncertainty in covariate summaries. Second, we develop a new transportability method that allows more flexible modeling of covariate shift, thereby accounting for covariate shift and uncertainty in covariate summaries simultaneously. Asymptotic normality for the proposed estimator is established and its asymptotic variance is consistently estimated. The proposed method offers greater flexibility in accounting for covariate shift and thus permits consistent estimation and valid inference when the validity of entropy balancing is not guaranteed. The proposed methods are evaluated by simulations and illustrated with an analysis of Surveillance, Epidemiology, and End Results breast cancer data.
item.dc:creator: Ying Sheng, Yifei Sun, Chiung-Yu Huang

item.title: Claims, Designs, and Guarantees: A Critical Narrative Review of Statistical Inference Reform and Practice, 2016--2026
item.description: arXiv:2603.22594v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Statistics helps scientists decide what their data show, but its most familiar tool, the $p$-value, is widely misunderstood. Between 2016 and 2026, professional bodies issued new guidance, and researchers developed or popularised alternatives and complements: compatibility intervals, equivalence tests, Bayes factors, and e-values that remain valid when data are checked repeatedly. Reporting rules for trials and reviews were also rewritten. Yet practice has changed little: in the biomedical literature, about 96\% of papers that report $p$-values still include at least one below 0.05. This review argues that much of the confusion comes from treating these numbers as interchangeable. Each inferential procedure carries an intended interpretation and, where applicable, a formal guarantee, such as a 5\% false-alarm rate, that holds only if the study was run and analysed in a particular way. We call this the Claim--Design--Guarantee framework: a result licenses a claim only when the claim, the design (assignment, sampling, monitoring, selection, and analysis), and the guarantee of the method are aligned. We trace the main developments of the decade, explain each tool in plain terms with formal details in boxes, and show with reproducible examples when the choice of tool changes the conclusion. For example, in a simulated two-group study with 100 interim looks, repeatedly applying an unadjusted $p<0.05$ rule produced false positives in 37.6\% of studies, whereas the particular anytime-valid e-value procedure we used produced 2.2\%, below its theoretical 5\% upper bound. We end with a decision tree, a method-selection table, and a step-by-step workflow linked to current reporting guidelines.
item.dc:creator: Aswini Kumar Patra, Shashi Bhushan Jha

item.title: Kernel-based independence and mean independence tests for weakly dependent data
item.description: arXiv:2604.28104v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We provide a unified framework for independence and mean independence tests based on the Hilbert-Schmidt independence criterion, extending some previous results in the literature to hold in general topological spaces. We also present a complete theoretical analysis of the test statistic asymptotic behavior when the observed sample corresponds to a partial sample path of some stationary and ergodic stochastic process under near epoch dependence assumptions. In particular, we explore the test statistic consistency and limit distribution under both fixed and local hypothesis. The finite sample performance of the test(s) is illustrated with a succinct simulation study involving functional data.
item.dc:creator: Daniel Diz-Castro, Manuel Febrero-Bande, Wenceslao Gonz\'alez-Manteiga

item.title: Stabilised weighted data subsampling for accelerated Bayesian inference in models with recursive likelihoods
item.description: arXiv:2605.13397v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Bayesian inference for models with recursively defined likelihoods is computationally demanding, limiting scalability to large datasets.
